#1452. Luke Graham seizes his chance to shine in Scotland back-line... now Stoke defender aims to make himself a fixture for years to come

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.

In five matches to date in the Nations League, the manager has not yet been able to select the same back-three in two consecutive outings. Injuries and suspensions have seen to that.

For all that, you sense that even if he’d had a full quota of players to choose from, Pocognoli would still be figuring out his preferred defensive grouping.

This does feel like a time of opportunity for those who are fresh on the scene. Catch the eye and there’s a real chance to become established as a mainstay of the team moving forward.

Luke Graham did his chances of doing just that no harm at all in his first start and second cap for his country on Friday.

Playing in between Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney, the Stoke City man made a compelling case to stay there with a strong and diligent display.

Luke Graham enjoyed a composed debut for Scotland as they recorded a much-needed win

On the back of a summer move from Dundee to the English Championship, Graham appears to have taken the step-up to international level in his stride.

‘It’s something I’ve always wanted to do since I was growing up, so I have to be ready for the moment and take it when it comes,’ he said.

‘I think there’s good competition. We have a lot of good centre-halves. Obviously, it was unfortunate for Welshy (Stephen Welsh) and Binksy (Luis Binks) to go out with injury, but that opens up a space for me to come in and try to cement a place.

‘When you’re out on that pitch, you have to do everything you can to try and stay in the team. I gave my all and I’ll just need to wait and see what happens going forward.’

Timing can be vital in football. And it’s conceivable that Graham’s might just propel him to become a Scotland regular.

While playing at Dens Park saw him mentioned in dispatches with regards to a call-up, his move to England, coming just before Pocognoli was announced as Steve Clarke’s successor, has seen his dream quickly become reality.

‘I’ve always said that one thing I wanted to do in my career was play for Scotland, so to get it over the line was pretty special,’ he reflected.

Former Dundee defender Graham proudly belts out the national anthem ahead of kick-off

‘Not much is going wrong for me at the moment, so it’s just about maintaining that and keeping it going every week.

‘I wouldn’t say I merited a start as we have a lot of good players in the camp. It’s up to the manager to pick the team and, luckily, he gave me the chance.

‘He just said to go out and enjoy it and do what you’re doing every week at Stoke. I think I did all right.’

Notwithstanding how limited the North Macedonians were on the night, Pocognoli was entitled to take encouragement from the way the back three acquitted themselves.

Playing closer to each other than we’d seen in the previous matches, they were rarely unpicked by balls through the middle. Angus Gunn was not overworked in goal. Tellingly, the only concession of the night came when Scott McTominay lost his man at a corner.

‘I think a lot of it is just being brave,’ Graham reflected. ‘It’s about bravery in going man-to-man with the striker, being brave on the ball, trying to break the lines and keeping possession.

‘So, I think bravery is the main thing and concentration as well.’

Graham keeps a close eye on North Macedonian danger man Elmin Rastoder at Hampden

With the defence solid enough, Pocognoli had a platform for a much-needed win. While the narrow scoreline made the final moments more anxious than they should have been, on balance, Scotland were deserved winners.

‘It’s just about winning games at this stage of the competition, so that was good,’ said Graham. ‘I think, if I’m being harsh, we should have killed the game off before it got to 1-1. We had a few good chances to put them to bed.

‘Then we kinda shot ourselves in the foot by conceding from a set piece. But Ben Gannon-Doak does well for the penalty and for us to go 2-1 up and see it out was good.’

No one would dispute that the display was a long way from perfect. There’s significant room for improvement ahead of the concluding group match with Switzerland on Monday.

‘We’re going through a bit of a transitional spell at the minute, so it’s not going to be all smooth sailing from the get-go,’ Graham said. ‘It’s about adjusting and trying to build on performances in every game. I think it’s going to take time.

‘It’s a different style, a different manager and we just have to keep being patient. You look at the squad now and there’s a lot of new, young players coming through. It’s just about encouraging us young boys and showing we can get a place in the squad.

‘It is going to take time but, once we get there, we’re going to do really well and compete right at the top of the game.’

Graham has been a huge success in Stoke's flying start to the Championship season

Graham does look like he’s moving in the right direction. From watching Scotland compete at the World Cup on licensed premises five months ago, he hopes he too can be the toast of the nation one day.

‘I didn’t go. It was too expensive for me,’ he explained. ‘I think I was just like everyone else, watching in the pub with their mates. It was pretty amazing and hopefully I can be part of something like that one day.

‘I wasn’t too far away (previously), I think. Steve Clarke, the former manager, told me that. It’s just about trusting myself now and hopefully getting there one day.

‘There’s been a lot of hard work and dedication which has led me to this point. I’m very grateful to a lot of people who have helped me in my career so far and just to get this chance is amazing.’

#1451. US Supreme Court rebuffs White House effort to cut research grants

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up a dispute over federal research grants hands a win to scientists.Credit: Kevin Dietsch/Getty

The US Supreme Court has dealt a blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to terminate research grants it deemed at odds with its political priorities.

The court said today that it would, for now, not intervene in a landmark legal battle over the cancellation of research grants by the US National Science Foundation (NSF) and four other federal agencies. The court’s decision leaves in place several lower-court rulings that came out this year and last and required the reinstatement of hundreds of cancelled awards while a lawsuit brought by a group of scientists against the government proceeds.

Since early 2025, US President Donald Trump’s administration has cancelled thousands of grants from agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the NSF. Many of the cancelled grants were for studies that contained terms that the administration said ran counter to its priorities, such as “climate change,” “equity” and “gender”. In response, a group of University of California researchers whose grants had been terminated sued the administration. Lower courts have repeatedly sided with the scientists, finding that the government had penalized academic researchers based on their viewpoints and that this likely violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and other activities.

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

The Supreme Court’s refusal to hear the case is a relief to scientists whose work was left in limbo, and leaves protections for their reinstated funding in place. “The denial is terrific news,” says Claudia Polsky, a lawyer for the University of California researchers. The denial came only three days after the case was considered on 13 November, and none of the nine justices publicly dissented from the decision. “Those are all of the best signs one could have that the Supreme Court really did not buy the government's argument,” Polsky says.

The White House referred Nature to the US Department of Justice, which said that it would “continue to litigate” the order by one of the lower courts that “currently prevents the cancellation of certain federal research grants supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives within the University of California system”.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up the case now is not the final word on grant terminations. The lower courts found that the researchers were likely to succeed, rather than issuing a final judgment. Once a final ruling is issued, it could be appealed, potentially bringing the case back before the Supreme Court.

The case kicked off in June 2025, when Neeta Thakur, a physician who studies marginalized communities, and five other researchers at the University of California who had had federal grants terminated sued the Trump administration. The researchers argued that the cancellations were arbitrary and unlawfully penalized scientists whose work clashed with the White House’s political agenda.

The same month, judge Rita Lin at the US District Court for the Northern District of California ordered the NSF, the Environmental Protection Agency and the National Endowment for the Humanities to reinstate the University of California researchers’ grants. The plaintiffs had a “substantial likelihood that their funding was terminated based on the viewpoint expressed in their grant proposals”, Lin wrote.

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

In August 2025, the Supreme Court issued a ruling in a separate case about the termination of around 800 NIH grants. The court ruled that federal district courts — such as the one that originally ruled in favour of Thakur — cannot reinstate cancelled grants by invoking a law called the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires federal agencies to follow proper procedures and justify their decisions. Some lower courts had used this reasoning to reinstate terminated grants.

#1450. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli urges Ben Gannon-Doak to improve his end product but insists he's happy with progress of mercurial winger

Published: 17:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has backed Ben Gannon-Doak to find his killer instinct in the final third and establish himself as Scotland’s main man.

The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.

But, as has been the case throughout his Scotland career, the 21-year-old’s final ball in key moments left a lot to be desired.

Pocognoli is under no illusions that Gannon-Doak still has plenty to improve on, but insists that it won’t be long before things start to click for the talented youngster.

‘As long as he is high on the pitch and is creating one v ones I am happy,’ said the Belgian. ‘With Ben, we know that he is at a young age and needs to work on specific things.

‘On Friday, he had great opportunities. We know that he needs to improve on the end product, but he created a penalty and against Slovenia and North Macedonia away he created a number of unbelievable one v ones.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets Ben Gannon-Doak as he is substituted at Hampden

‘He did that last night as well. We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball. I am happy with his performance.

‘He is a young lad, just 21. Okay, he has become more mature than he was, but I believe in one moment he will have a click about decision making.

‘I believe if he is playing every game he can make many decisions. He will know that in the next game he will have to do it again.

‘If he knows that he only has to play a game every two weeks, sometimes he can think, “This is my moment”.

‘It is a process. He will become older and at some point will become relaxed in his decision making, but at this very young age what he is producing is very good.

‘I say exactly the same thing to him after training on the pitch. I say, “Ben, this is the next step”. He knows that and it is important he knows that.’

Scotland conclude their Nations League campaign in Switzerland on Monday knowing that only a victory against the group winners will be enough if they are to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia – currently one point better off ahead of their trip to North Macedonia – into second spot.

Pocognoli admits Gannon-Doak's end product has to improve after another frustrating show

Should that happen, Scotland would have a crack at earning promotion to League A via a play-off in March, and also crucially guarantee their place as a Pot 2 side for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

‘We are still alive in this competition,’ said Pocognoli, who celebrated his first win at Hampden on Friday at the third time of asking. ‘We know we have to do more than this competition. This competition is about trying to build something.

‘But it is nice to have that possibility on Monday to try to create something against one of the top 20 teams in the world.

‘We need to try to be brave. Switzerland have already qualified so let’s go there and be smart because they are a good team.

‘It is part of the process to play away against a top team. That is not something we have done yet. The approach will be different and, for me as a coach, it is a game with a lot of responsibility.’

#1449. Michael Carrick will not survive unless Manchester United change

Sometimes comments, however over the top, hit home. Michael Carrick will desperately hope the remark from his former Manchester United team-mate Gary Neville is not one of them. That it does not stick. That it does not come to define his time in charge of United this season – if he lasts this season. Or be used in one of those highlight reels, with doom-laden music, to explain the story of this Premier League campaign.

On TV co-commentary duty for Sky, Neville referred to United as “blue mannequins” (they were wearing their away kit) and said that for a period after half-time it was the worst he had ever seen them play since he started watching, aged five. Neville is now 51. That is a lot of games to settle on this conclusion so strongly and, surely, inaccurately.

"They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville says Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh

But so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the plan to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

We now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

It is not just that. Last year, United revamped their attack. Benjamin Sesko was absent through injury but are Cunha – despite his goal – Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford actually showing they are good enough? They, too, are passive and do not effect the play. Do not have that killer instinct. There is then an over-reliance on Fernandes. And if he does not do it, then who steps up?

That 15 minutes after half-time that culminated in the Martínez mishap was certainly woeful. But despite going close, United were also second best in the opening period, with Fulham’s 19-year-old academy product Josh King showing why he was so close to a senior England call-up. The forward ran riot, tormenting left-back Luke Shaw and was only denied by Senne Lammens. On more than one occasion, especially with a smart save with his right boot.

The goalkeeper was at the centre of Fulham’s goal, which was a shambles that summed up the state of United, who are just too easy to play against. And, so, Fulham’s captain Calvin Bassey was too strong for Cunha, who threw himself to the ground, looking for a foul, losing the ball from Kobbie Mainoo’s easy pass. The defender strode forward before Lammens parried his low shot, which then bounced off Martínez and back past the goalkeeper and into the net.

It was a Hammersmith End House of Horrors for United. To cap it all, Martínez then tried to blame Lammens who had, frankly, kept United in the game up until that point and could legitimately have told him where to go. And asked why he could not trap a ball and clear.

"A horror at the Hammersmith end!"Lisandro Martínez puts the ball into his own net and Fulham lead! 😯 pic.twitter.com/jDmY4zL2XN

Fulham will certainly feel their own frustration. But with their new head coach Álvaro Arbeloa and an evolving team – if only striker Gonzalo García was more deadly – there are clear signs of optimism, having also just drawn at Liverpool.

United’s late equaliser was fortunate. Yes, they applied pressure but to no real effect until Cunha’s shot deflected off the boot of Fulham defender David Affengruber as he tried to block, to wrong-foot goalkeeper Bernd Leno, who had also been outstanding. It was credited to Cunha, his first of the season, and the relief from Carrick was understandably palpable.

Manchester United are LEVEL! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DCxwlrzf1M

But, once again, it was not up to the standard needed. And beyond the point, beyond the avoidance of defeat, that is the reality of where United are right now under Carrick who needs to step up, take more responsibility. And, like his team, be far less passive. Otherwise, he will not last.

Might these games offer less possession and more counter-attacking chances? That’s glass half full.

I was purely referring to the fact that they walked around the pitch. I’ve never seen a Manchester United team walk around on the pitch that much.

Michael has got to stop defending them. I get why he wants to defend them, he’s loyal, and there’s a long way to go into the season.

Both teams were the same, I called them mannequins. I’ve never seen United walk around so much out of possession, no alertness, no being on your toes.

I wish he could play those attacking players, but they are going to kill him defensively.

Neville goes on to call that period: “An absolute disgrace, nowhere near good enough.”

"They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville says Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh

I know Manchester United have a lot of individual quality, I have played against them for many years and know them really well. I know to be alert in case they shoot from distance. When you make some saves in the game you feel very focused. Unfortunately I couldn’t keep out the goal but that is football.

I didn’t think we were. Did you think we were? Football is a difficult game. We controlled a lot of the first half. It’s the Premier League and you will have spells where you don’t have it all your own way. To expect total dominance for the whole game, I don’t think anyone gets that in this league.

I thought we should have won the game, I thought we created enough to win the game. The goal we did concede is one of them goals. The boys could have thought it is one of those days but I really like the reaction. We nearly won it in the end. We came to get the win of course, the way it panned out and the way we finished is the positive we take from it.

I think we did a good game. Obviously not an easy game for us, we were in the bottom position but we saw personality with the ball, we were brave. We had moments where we had to defend but in general we did a good game.

We wanted to control the transition and the counter attacks. We know they put too many people inside so we have to control the space behind our midfielders. They sometimes found the spaces, it is a difficult match against a big team and for me they will be near the top of the league by the end of the season.

Now we have to find the first victory. If you see our first five games we have already played Man Utd, Chelsea, at Anfield, at Sunderland. Now we have an October that will be so important for us.

There were so many things for them, you can see it in the foul by [Harry] Maguire. Every decision was for them. I knew after the game against Manchester City that they don’t like Manchester United to lose.

It’s hard to explain, I feel after the first half we always get a lot of chances and create, play well.

In the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us and we cannot accept this. We always play better after conceding goal, and it cannot be like this.

I don’t think today was about final decisions, we were a bit unlucky, I hit the post, and Bruno hit the post. We need to create more and hope the luck comes and we score. We need to improve in every single position.

It was too slow, Fulham ran more and looked like they wanted to win more. Bassey just eased Cunha out the way [for Fulham’s goal] and looked like he wanted to take the game to Man United and Carrick will be thinking ‘we need to do a lot more’.

It was a game that was a real struggle for both teams. Both lacked confidence. There were challenges for both managers coming into this game, they both need the international break to start their seasons again.

The defensive work from both teams was awful and lacked effort. Carrick will be relieved going back to Manchester with a goal and a point.

Manchester United play Spurs when the Premier League returns in three weeks, in a game that will feel huge.

5 - With five points, this is Manchester United's joint-lowest tally after five games of a Premier League season, also picking up five in 2014-15.Sluggish. pic.twitter.com/UZTBWRpGnm

Fulham remain winless but the draw lifts them above Spurs, who will spend the international break at the foot of the table. It is just one win in five for United, and it was another performance which was far from convincing. It could have been worse though, they were a few minutes away from losing. On this evidence, both of these teams are in for a struggle relative to expectations.

Fulham wanted a free-kick on the edge of the box for a sliding challenge on Kevin for Maguire but the referee decides he got the ball.

United break forward and win a corner. It comes for Martinez who shifts his feet to shoot with his right foot and the goal-bound effort was blocked!

Just the three minutes of added time to play, but United are the team pushing forward searching for an unlikely winner.

United may have just spared themselves a damaging defeat, and there might just be time to go on an win this. Cunha with a speculative shot from outside the box, and Affengruber extends his left leg to block the shot but the deflection leaves Leno stranded. A stroke of luck for United but Fulham have invited it.

Manchester United are LEVEL! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DCxwlrzf1M

Bassey now penalised for a high boot on Dalot, United free-kick on the halfway line. Fulham just about standing firm, and they are helped when a crossfield pass towards Dorgu bounces off for a throw-in.

United with another corner and there are loud appeals for a handball penalty against Bassey, the proximity was very close but his hand was up. But VAR takes a look and the fact the hand was tucked in towards his chest spares the Fulham defender.

Fulham and the home crowd happy with a goal kick after an overhit cross towards Shaw at the back post. Dorgu has been sent on in Carrick’s last throw of the dice, replacing Shaw at left-back.

You would not say United are pulling Fulham from pillar to post, it feels a little hopeful, but it is one-way traffic. An attack against defence session in Fulham’s half. Charles and Kevin do well to relieve the pressure momentarily, but United are back on the attack again.

Here are those changes: Mason Mount on for Kobbie Mainoo for United, while Andersen replaces King for the home team. Arbeloa happy to hold what he has. Lisandro Martinez volleys a shot over the bar.

Positive first involvement from Zirkzee, releasing Mbeumo, but the Fulham defenders read his intentions and blocked the shot after he cut inside. Joachim Andersen is preparing to come on for Fulham, as is Mason Mount for United.

Much better from Fulham, another attack started by Bassey reading play just like the goal, but this time Lammens’s wrists were strong to parry Kevin’s shot. Rashford is then flagged offside.

Fulham change: Larsson is on for Berge, Sweden for Norway. And Carrick has brought on Zirkzee for Rashford. Famous last words, but does that make you more likely to score a goal? Not that Rashford can feel hard done to.

Fulham have stopped playing since they scored, and they needed Leno again to tip a Cunha shot around the post. The United forward was falling over, but he generated enough power to trouble the goalkeeper. From the corner, Maguire picks up the ball on the far side and chips a cross over the blue shirts in the middle.

Kevin sold himself in a one-on-one with Rashford, but King did well to put his foot in at the edge of the box and the ball bounces through kindly to Leno. Tielemans then misplaces a pass when United were in a promising position.

If United had played like this from the start of the second half they would not be losing, but now they have just 20 minutes plus stoppage time to overturn the deficit.

Fulham making a double sub: Kevin and Palacios on for Iwobi and Bobb.

United have roused themselves since conceding, winning a flurry of corners.

What a save from Leno! Mbeumo’s curling shot from outside the box was arcing beautifully into the far corner, but the German goalkeeper tipped his effort around the post.

Then Maguire is eased out at the back post, and Fulham breathe a sigh of relief.

Strong words from Gary Neville after the goal went it: “I’ve watched United since the age of five and that is the worst 15 minutes [from half-time to the goal] I have seen them play.”

Well doesn’t that just sum up United’s season so far. There are appeals for a foul on Cunha from Bassey, but the Fulham defender was stronger and he took some initiative to drive towards the box. Bassey let fly and kept his shot down, Lammens could only stick out a leg and the ball rebounded off the helpless Martinez and back into the net.

"A horror at the Hammersmith end!"Lisandro Martínez puts the ball into his own net and Fulham lead! 😯 pic.twitter.com/jDmY4zL2XN

Fulham have a corner after it opened up nicely for Iwobi at the edge of the box, but his left-footed strike deflects behind. A very smooth footballer, but finishing has never been Iwobi’s strong suit. Fulham fail to make anything of the corner.

Fulham and United’s fans now urging their teams on after the game halted to glacial pace. Nothing much happening at all since the start of the second half.

Gary Neville growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of intensity out of possession by both teams: “Never walk on a football pitch.” Questions have been asked of United’s fitness levels and physical readiness for the new season. Fulham enjoying a spell of possession in United’s half again.

More from Neville: “It’s like it’s time for the whites to play against the blue mannequins, before they reverse it up the other end. One thing I do know, I’ve played in a lot of football matches, it’s not right.”

There has been a real lack of conviction in Rashford’s play in the final third, this time it was underhit pass across the box towards Mbeumo which was cut out. Good ball by Tielemans to release Rashford, but no end product again.

Sir Alex Ferguson is watching on at Craven Cottage. The game has slipped into one of its lulls again.

Nice football from Fulham involving Charles and Iwobi but United break forward after a loose touch by Bobb. Fernandes did well to keep the ball and wait for support, and Castagne is booked for a block on Rashford.

The first few minutes of the half are played deep in Fulham’s territory, but United’s delivery from wide is not good enough and Cunha is penalised for a foul in the middle in any case.

At half-time that is another worrying performance from Manchester United. Yes, they could be ahead and have created chances, with Bruno Fernandes hitting the post. But on the balance of play they should be behind with Fulham’s 19-year-old Josh King the best player on the pitch and United reliant on goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Michael Carrick has more work to do during the interval than Fulham’s Alvaro Arbeloa and cannot be happy with how defensively vulnerable his team and but also how wasteful they are in front of goal.

Both teams will believe they should have scored in that first half in a game that has oscillated between periods of passivity and flurries of goal-mouth action. When United speed up their interplay, it looks like they can cut through Fulham, but Carrick’s team’s box defending leaves much to be desired. There were 26 shots on goal without reward in that 45 minutes.

Another chance is missed, this time Rashford with a side foot over the bar from a Cunha cross that took a nick on the way through. Always leaning back, poor technique from a player of his standing.

Fulham then throw a punch back, but King is booked for diving after pushing the ball beyond Maguire. The attacker is not happy, but not sure he can have any complaints.

United almost caught out by a one-two between Iwobi and Garcia, but Lammens rushes off his line to get there first. Both attacks look to have the beating of both defences, but somehow there have been no goals.

United’s best move of the game, starting with a whipped pass from Tielemans when under pressure into Dalot who turns into space inside. Fernandes could have taken a shot on himself from the edge of the box, but he moved the ball on to Rashford but his side-foot shot was tame and straight at Leno.

The game has settled after that flurry of chances when both teams could easily have scored. Fulham do well to block Rashford’s sight of goal as he cuts inside looking for a shot, and then Mbeumo commits a foul.

Cunha with a deflected strike from distance, which arcs over Leno and glances off the post! The sort of deflection that gives a goalkeeper no chance, Leno was scrambling.

Mainoo’s shot is blocked from the corner, and then Fulham break forward with numbers. Iwobi picks out Josh King in the box, and Lammens sticks out a right leg to keep out his driven shot.

Josh King is again showing why he was so close to a full England call-up. The 19-year-old is at the heart of the action as Fulham continue to create chance after chance against a very shaky Manchester United defence who have been reliant on goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

Fulham respond, with Robinson’s cross looping to the back post to the unmarked King but he could not get over the side-foot volley and it was a comfortable save from Lammens.

This stop was less comfortable though: Lammens plunges to his right to keep out a dig by Sander Berge from the edge of the box. It came after Garcia kicked fresh air in the area.

Then Bobb collects the ball in space at the edge of the box and is able to turn but he dragged his shot wide.

The home team and crowd have burst into life.

Fernandes hits the post for United! He should score, and it was poor defending from Fulham. Affengruber ran beyond the ball and was rolled by Cunha who was able to drive into the box, and he pulled the ball back for Fernandes who dragged his shot a touch, and it rebounded off the foot of the post.

Bruno Fernandes hits the post! 😬 pic.twitter.com/jMzn8ZyoYa

Better from United, turning the screw around the Fulham box but neither Mainoo nor Rashford fashion room for a shot, and then Dalot shoots wide from 25 yards with his weaker left foot.

Josh King finding space off the shoulder of United’s midfield again, but his shot from a tight angle is always rising. United are asking for trouble though if Fulham’s most creative player keeps collecting the ball in those spaces

United then come forward, with Robinson selling himself against Mbeumo, but Rashford cannot get over the header at the back post.

Fulham with a smooth passage of play from deep, finding space down United’s right and Garcia had made a dangerous run between Maguire and Martinez. Iwobi looked for his team-mate, but the ball glanced off his foot as he tried to direct it towards goal.

The interesting thing about Manchester United’s attack is that while they are all, clearly, individually good players do they actually do enough to warrant their status at the club? The truth is Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford simply have to do more and dominate games. We are yet to see that form them this season and, apart from Lisandro Martinez forcing a fine save from Bernd Leno, Fulham have carried the greater threat here.

Fulham have a corner after Josh King used his body well against Shaw. There has been lots of cat and mouse so far, both teams trying to play patiently from deep and the out of possession team lying in wait for a mistake. United clear the Fulham corner.

Bassey defends well in the area, but United are starting to warm to their task. Tielemans lifts a dangerous cross into the box, and Fernandes’s header deflects off Affengruber and behind for a corner.

A short corner comes to nothing, but from a second or possibly third phase Lisandro Martinez lets fly from distance with a swerving, outside of the left foot shot. Appeared destined for the corner, but Leno pushed the ball around the post. Great try from Martinez.

United have settled on the ball now, enjoying some possession of their own in non-threatening areas. Neither team appears too interested in gambling on the high press, a degree of wariness in their approaches. That was a nice Fulham move, sweeping from right to left, but Iwobi chipped a cross into Lammens’s gloves. Tielemans then looks for the run of Rashford with a through ball, but the forward is offside. Plenty of green grass behind Fulham’s back four though.

Fulham move the ball well again, Robinson setting the ball back for Garcia to strike from just outside the box but he dragged his shot wide of the near post. Too much time and space for the forward if you are United inclined, though. Tielemans then passes the ball out of play, splitting the difference between Dalot and Mbeumo.

Promising signs for Josh King as he carries the ball from the right touchline into a dangerous central position, unchallenged by United’s midfield. The home team have monopolised the ball so far, United sitting off in a shape, perhaps waiting for an error and the chance to counter-attack.

United get the game under way at Craven Cottage.

Very difficult to predict what you are going to be served by either of these teams. Both of their seasons are on a knife edge even at the this early juncture.

If Manchester United could choose a Premier League away fixture to revitalise their season, Fulham would be it. Not just because they are bottom of the league with just one point, albeit impressively earned last week away to Liverpool, but because United have not been beaten at Craven Cottage since December 2009 – although, not such a good omen for United, is the fact that Michael Carrick was in their team that day (playing at centre-back).

Michael Carrick dismissed as “ridiculous” any suggestion that his job as Manchester United’s head coach was at risk this early in the season. But he needs a positive result today against Fulham otherwise much of the prolonged international break will be taken up by debate as to whether he is up to it. United do not play again after today until they host stricken Tottenham Hotspur on October 10 and their start to this season has simply not been good enough. The concern for Carrick appears his inability to positively affect games when things are going against United.

JJ Gabriel has been in the news this week, and Sam Wallace writes in his column this week that the battle to sign up and coming academy players is growing ever more fierce between Premier League clubs. Managers are handing out debuts earlier and earlier to satisfy the demands of the best young players, and an increasing number of clubs are happy to gamble significant fees and wages on potental.

Fulham starting XI: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, King, Bobb, Iwobi, Garcia

Subs: Lecomte, Andersen, Palacios, Muniz, Kevin, Larsson, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon. Smith Rowe

Here's how The Fulham shape up. ⚪️ pic.twitter.com/0IxS0J3ldf

United starting XI: Lammens, Dalot, Martinez, Maguire, Shaw, Mainoo, Tielemans, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha, Rashford

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Zirkzee, Dorgu, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Heaven, Baleba, Lacey.

Presenting your United XI to face Fulham ✊

The script pretty much writes itself these days. A flicker of optimism and hope of a fresh start giving way to the same old frustrations, complaints and inquests, the cumulative toll of which places an ever greater strain on a club mired in mediocrity but with little reprieve from the expectations that come with bearing such an illustrious name.

Michael Carrick says Pro Ref’s apology over the derby fiasco means little to Manchester United – but warned his players they cannot allow such setbacks to derail their season.

Chief refereeing officer Howard Webb formally apologised to United after the VAR officials Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus failed to spot Enzo Fernandez was offside before wrongly allowing Erling Haaland’s winning goal to stand in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory at Old Trafford.

United were left shocked by the scale of the blunder, which came with 30 minutes of the game remaining and City already down to 10 men.

But Carrick has told his players not to become preoccupied with such injustices as they bid to overcome their poor start to the season before a crucial trip to Craven Cottage.

“It can have an impact in the moment of time, it can have a big impact, but we can’t let it have an impact on the rest of the season,” the United manager said.

“That’s for us to get back to winning ways as soon as possible. Listen, one-off things can happen, at the time it was a pretty big one, we know that. I don’t think I need to go over that.

“But yeah, I’ve got faith in it [VAR], it’s the system that we work towards and that we use so the apology doesn’t mean an awful lot.”

Carrick added: “I can appreciate and I respect it for them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong, I think it happens - it does happen.

“But moving forward, yeah, we just have to deal with it, what’s thrown in front of us. And maybe we get one or two decisions on the back of how it balances out - percentages or law of averages or whatever that may be.

“But that was a pretty big one to take and had a huge impact on that game and that’s why it was particularly tough.”

Michael Carrick may have had a point when he said it was “ridiculous” to question his future this early in the season, but this afternoon’s game at Fulham will shape the mood at Manchester United for the next three weeks.

A tally of four points from their first four games of the season is a disappointing start, and Brighton added to the sense of gloom in the League Cup by becoming the first side in 50 years to win from 2-0 down at Old Trafford.

With Champions League football on the agenda, that competition was at the bottom of United’s priority list but the ragged nature of the performance prompted boos around the stadium.

The no-show at Hull and defeat to 10-man City also fall into the “it’s how you lose” category of defeat, while there are widening fissures between the fanbase and the club’s hierarchy over ticketing policy and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s political interventions.

The mood has also been sour at Fulham in the first few weeks of the season. In fact, they start the game bottom of the Premier League with one point, but do have the incentive of knowing a draw would take them above Spurs.

Following reports of friction between some established players and new head coach Alvaro Arbeloa though, they produced their best performance of the season in a goalless draw at Anfield last week when they had chances to win the game.

Fulham made nine changes in the League Cup in mid-week, but still ran out 3-2 winners at West Ham. Despite the west London club being an established mid-table Premier League team for a number of seasons, and United’s vulnerable state for the past few years, Fulham have beaten their opponent’s just once in the league since December 2009.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1448. John McGinn warns Tartan Army it might take 18 MONTHS for Scotland to click into gear under new boss Pocognoli

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

Steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ said the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most important thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create big chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’

If that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’

Give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’

Even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli

‘We need to play slightly better,’ he said. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s important that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’

Friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both said the most important thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high

Tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

‘Difficult,’ said McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’

#1447. 'Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It's my first time in Old Trafford!' - An afternoon with my 10-year-old inside the Theatre of Screams for Carrick's last stand

Published: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!)

You can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

That will just set you back £25.  For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium

No wonder Big Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his plans to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his new stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

The crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

The 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

#1446. As El Niño builds, studies of extreme marine heatwaves must start now

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alistair J. Hobday is a chief research scientist at CSIRO Environment, Hobart, Australia.

Kathryn E. Smith is a research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Claire M. Spillman is a principal research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Karen Filbee-Dexter is a Future Fellow at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and a principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Neil J. Holbrook is a professor of ocean and climate dynamics at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century, University of Tasmania, Hobart, Australia.

Caroline Rowland is head of ocean cryosphere and climate at the Met Office, Exeter, UK.

Dan A. Smale is a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Grant Smith is a senior research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Mads S. Thomsen is an adjunct professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and an associate professor in the School of Biological Sciences, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand.

Thomas Wernberg is a laureate professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Alex Sen Gupta is a professor in the Climate Change Research Centre and the Centre for Marine Science and Innovation, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia.

Coral nurseries, such as this one in French Polynesia, can be used to study the resilience of the organisms in real-world settings. Credit: Alexis Rosenfeld/Getty

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean at record-high levels and forecasts of an extreme El Niño climate event, intense marine heatwaves are expected around the world in the coming year1,2. Scientists must prepare to study these extreme conditions now, so that managers of marine resources and decision makers can develop and implement response strategies and communities can plan for a hotter future.

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

El Niño is part of a recurring natural cycle in Earth’s climate in which warmer waters in the central and eastern Pacific alter ocean and atmospheric circulation, affecting weather worldwide. Marine heatwaves associated with El Niño provide opportunities to study ecosystems under real-world stress conditions and on scales that cannot be replicated in a laboratory.

Marine heatwaves can be forecast weeks or months ahead, giving researchers time to design field studies, deploy instruments and collect baseline data. Investigations can be designed to test theories and improve our understanding of ecological processes, thresholds and recovery mechanisms in a rapidly warming ocean.

Such knowledge can inform decisions about how to manage marine resources, such as whether to close fisheries. Much has been learnt about marine heatwaves since the last El Niño, in 2023–24 (see ‘Hot water’). But these lessons need to be consolidated and scaled up into consistent, long-term preparedness plans.

Source: Climate Reanalyzer (CC-BY-4.0); go.nature.com/4zae69a

Fortunately, effective approaches established in one place can be extended to others. Australia is a leader in developing early-warning systems and response plans for adaptation to a more extreme ocean climate. Other nations (including the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Peru) have improved their awareness of these events and put in place observation systems, forecasts and briefings, policy mechanisms and (in a few cases) adaptation measures.

But further action is needed, particularly in locations that have previously been unaffected by severe marine heatwaves. Here, we highlight seven priorities in increasing marine heatwave preparedness.

Seasonal forecasts with lead times of several months are now being delivered in various regions, including the United States3 and Australia4, and such systems are being developed in the United Kingdom and New Zealand5 and for the Mediterranean Sea6.

Forecasting relies on physical and statistical models to predict probable ocean temperatures7. Data from sustained surface and below-surface observations are essential for initializing models and verifying predictions, building users’ confidence in forecasts.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

But managers want to know more precisely what the duration and intensity of a marine heatwave is expected to be. Forecasts become less accurate the further ahead they look and at fine spatial scales, such as along coasts. Improved ocean monitoring, a better understanding of the drivers of marine heatwaves and continued refinements of model physics are needed to improve forecast accuracy7.

Advances in machine learning are expected to be transformative. Next-generation models that incorporate ocean physics might be able to predict unprecedented marine heatwaves more accurately than current technologies can. Downscaling global climate models to inshore regions using machine-learning techniques could also increase the usefulness of forecasts in places where most marine-resource users operate.

Planning for and communication about impending marine heatwaves are also improving1. In 2023, engagement was piecemeal and often only in response to events that were already in progress. Activities are now more proactive and structured.

Coordinated briefings that translate forecasts into action provide ways of engaging with affected groups and planning ahead. Such communication strategies should be implemented around the world4,8. National briefings provide a broad overview of marine heatwave risks and impacts. Regional and industry specialists can provide further local advice.

For example, Australia’s national marine climate briefing series4 has been running since 2023. Similar meetings (led or contributed to by some of us) have taken place for the western Pacific Ocean (G.S.) and in the United Kingdom (C.R.), Brazil (K.E.S.), Singapore (C.M.S.) and New Zealand (C.M.S.).

Seafood-producing firms and conservation managers need a menu of actions to choose from when a marine heatwave looms. Options include adjusting collection strategies, temporarily closing fisheries and modifying aquaculture operations1.

Australia has developed regional and industry-specific response plans for marine heatwaves8. Response teams for fisheries are active during warming events and provide coordinated mechanisms for assessment, communication and management actions4,9.

Impacts of marine heatwaves are being monitored in restored giant kelp forests in Tasmania, Australia.Credit: Scott Ling/University of Tasmania

Early-warning systems and interagency coordination are key components of timely responses. Industry has also adopted operating protocols to reduce the impacts of marine heatwaves on animal health and food-product quality. For example, abalone fisheries in New South Wales have changed how sea snails (Haliotis spp.) are fished, handled and prepared for live export10. Other regions could benefit from similar plans4.

For example, fishing of Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens), the source of around 20% of fishmeal and fish oil globally, has already been curbed by the current El Niño. In 2023, the fishery had to be closed, resulting in an estimated loss11 of US$1.4 billion. This year, an alert in February prompted Peruvian authorities to bring the fishing season forwards by two weeks and reduce the total allowable catch of anchoveta and white anchovy (Anchoa nasus) by more than 30% to 1.9 million tonnes. This meant that fisheries could catch about 450,000 tonnes before the heatwave intensified and the season was ended in May.

In 2023, marine heatwave preparedness was recognized as inadequate in most regions. The emphasis then was mainly on raising risk awareness in sectors such as fisheries and aquaculture1. However, these and other industries need to adapt to a changing ocean, too.

Awareness has now grown among sectors and institutions, and behaviours have begun to change. For example, Australian marine climate briefings draw engagement from aquaculture and fishery managers, marine tourism operators, policymakers, researchers and individual fishers4.

In the United States, forecasts of marine heatwaves trigger advice to fishers regarding increases in interactions with marine mammals as the overlap between animals’ hunting grounds and deployed fishing gear expands, which can result in fishery closures. Coral-reef managers involved in restoration efforts can scale back replanting efforts and start collecting genetic material.

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

In the Mediterranean Sea, limiting diving tourism at coral reefs to minimize damage during marine heatwaves has been proposed, mirroring practices that were adopted in Asia during the 2023–24 marine heatwaves11.

In the Cook Islands’ black-pearl industry, seasonal forecasts have been proposed for supporting decisions around adaptive management aimed at reducing the thermal stress of oysters. These include increased reliance on hatchery production under controlled temperature conditions and preferential harvesting of pearls during cooler periods of the year.

In the United Kingdom, a national marine heatwave network and code of best practice have been established, enabling the exchange of transdisciplinary knowledge. Similar transfers of experience, capacity and lessons learnt between jurisdictions can accelerate preparedness globally and help to embed risk management into routine decision-making processes4.

The 2023 El Niño led to calls to strengthen monitoring and research capacity to improve the detection of, understanding of and response to marine heatwaves. Observation networks are now becoming a core component of preparedness and response plans, providing the information needed to support forecasting, impact assessment, management interventions and long-term adaptation strategies12.

Targeted uses of gliders and intensified monitoring strategies can bolster research, situational awareness and management decisions12. Research has expanded into understanding ecological resilience and adaptation. For example, genetic studies are identifying traits that might enhance the capacity of key fishery or habitat-forming species13 to persist under increasing thermal stress.

#1445. England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel said the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel said, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about

This may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

It was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

Has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he said, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

Spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he said at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far

The England coach said more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

And for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, said on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice said on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’

Tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.
