#1396. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

#1395. Leeds Ditched Star Labelled ‘Worse Than Augustin’, Now He’s Scored 11 CL Goals

Leeds United have made some excellent signings in recent years, none more so than current club captain Ethan Ampadu, as well as England duo James Trafford and Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Ampadu has taken the jump from the Championship to the Premier League like a duck to water, while Trafford and Calvert-Lewin both have the quality to take Leeds to the next level after they consolidated their spot in the top flight in the first season after promotion.

Calvert-Lewin is even attracting interest from rivals Manchester United but, according to GIVEMESPORT sources, he is set to extend his contract to stay at Elland Road instead.

It's fair to say that, like many clubs, the Yorkshire outfit haven't always got it right with their transfer business.

There are already big doubts over summer addition Jean-Matteo Bahoya, who was viewed as an exciting signing but who has barely been picked by Daniel Farke, with the club already making a decision on terminating his loan spell in the January transfer window.

Bahoya isn't the only forward to be a flop, so far at least, at Elland Road in recent years, with Facundo Buonanotte and Jean-Kevin Augustin two more prime examples.

Leeds signed the former on loan from Brighton and Hove Albion in January of this year to boost their survival battle, but he played just 36 minutes of Premier League football between then and the end of the campaign, before returning to the Seagulls.

The story of Augustin is even more interesting, from a player who signed on loan from RB Leipzig, to one who ended up costing the Whites around £40m, despite playing only 48 minutes of football for them.

Leeds signed Augustin on loan with a £18m obligation to buy the player if they won promotion to the Premier League, although they argued that, because the Championship season had been interrupted due to the coronavirus pandemic and not completed until July, Augustin's contract should have reverted to Leipzig at the time they actually went up.

Leeds lost their appeal and agreed on a £15.5m compensation package with Leipzig, while they were also ordered to pay Augustin himself £24.5m in compensation because of the failed permanent transfer.

Augustin will undoubtedly go down as Leeds' worst ever signing for that reason and the number of minutes paid, but Leeds content creator Joe Wainman told GIVEMESPORT previously that Weston McKennie was 'arguably worse than Augustin'.

He said: "The mad thing is, I'm that vitriolic towards last season and the demise of the football club, with the poor acquisitions that we made and the coach that was in charge made in Jesse Marsch, that I would say with chest that Weston McKennie is arguably a worse signing than JKA, and JKA played about 15 minutes.

That's how strongly I feel about that. He seemed disinterested. We saw nowhere near the player that he's shown in the past, as you've mentioned.

That is a big statement that might have been in the heat of the moment, but there was no doubt that McKennie was a big disappointment at Elland Road.

Leeds signed the USA international on loan in January 2023 until the end of the season, with the option to make the deal permanent for ££30m.

Speaking on his arrival, McKennie when asked what he was going to bring, said: "Hard work, non-stop 90 minutes back and forth, tackles, trash talk probably and everything - funny moments and serious moments.

It's a dream come true, I've dreamed of playing in the Premier League for the longest time. To have the support system I have here, I'm ready.

Some Leeds fans would certainly question the work-rate they saw from the American in the final months of the season, as they were relegated from the Premier League and McKennie returned to his parent club.

Having failed to reach the levels he had done earlier in his career during his time in Yorkshire, it would have been a surprise to supporters that his career has continued on an upward trajectory, with the 28-year-old establishing himself as a key player for Juve.

McKennie scored nine goals and registered eight assists for the Serie A giants last term, including netting four times in the Champions League, taking his career total in the competition to 11.

McKennie may not be a well-loved figure at Leeds after the role he played in their demise that season, but he has shown the quality he has in his locker, which makes his Elland Road spell even more disappointing.

Erling Haaland delivered a monologue of over two minutes detailing the teams he represented in the years covered by the Premier League's investigation into Man City, as the star questioned how he was meant to respond to the club's guilty verdict.

Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed.

An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals.

Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

Haaland was quizzed about the club's situation by Norwegian broadcaster TV2, after scoring in the national team's 3-1 victory over Wales on Saturday.

The Man City star's initial answer lasted for two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges.

Erling Haaland insisted it was difficult for him to answer a question about Man City's guilty verdict, with the club appealing against the decision of an independent commission. Source: TV2Sport

Haaland stressed he remains happy at the club after being asked about his future given the potential ramificiations if Man City fail with their appeal to overturn the verdict.

'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland began.

'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle…

'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'

Haaland continued by listing fellow Norwegians who had been at Man City at the time, joking that they may be in a better place to offer insight.

'There were quite a few Norwegians at the club during that period, I think,' Haaland said.

'Abdisalam Ibrahim, Martin Samuelsen and Omar Elabdellaoui were there. Kjetil Haug was there too. I think there were a couple more but I can't remember.

The forward distanced himself from the case as he listed team he played from 2009-18, the time covered by the charges. Pictured: Haaland in action for Molde in 2018

'But it's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

'A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022 and a new nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024. I think that says everything about the matter. I'm a City player, and I'm incredibly happy there.'

Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Haaland, who has won eight major honours at the club including the Treble in 2023, was asked about whether the case has affected his thoughts on his Man City future.

'I understand that you want a little headline here, but as I said, I signed a long-term contract in 2024,' Haaland responded.

'I'd say I made a pretty good choice by joining City in 2022. We can all agree on that. I won't say it myself, but look at the trophies I've won and how I've developed on and off the pitch.

'I'm standing here after winning an international 3-1 and we're top of our group in Europe.

'Things aren't going so well for City in the league, but we'll try to turn that around against Fulham. But we can't focus on that now. Now we have to focus on Denmark.'

Man City have won twice and lost three times in the Premier League since the independent commission verdict was announced in September.

#1393. Raimondo: Frosinone stars reveals where he must improve to earn Italy call-up

Frosinone striker Antonio Raimondo says he must improve in two areas before earning a senior Italy call-up and names Euro 2020 winner Ciro Immobile as one of his role models.

Raimondo is one of Serie A’s top scorers this season, with eight goals in ten league games. The 22-year-old hasn’t yet received an Italy call-up and, perhaps, only a recent injury has kept him out of Roberto Mancini’s squad for the November break.

“I’m not thinking about expectations placed on me. When things go well, you are always good; when they don’t, you become the worst. I think it’s important to find balance,” Raimondo told Tuttosport.

When asked about his role models, the Frosinone star replied: “Cavani, Icardi and Immobile. Three fantastic strikers, and I’d like to take something from all of them. I still watch games of great players to study their movements and understand their mindset: being clinical in front of goal, how to attack space, or move into open field.”

Raimondo already discussed a potential Italy call-up in previous interviews, so what does he need to do to finally fulfil his dream?

“I must keep doing what I’m doing – he replied – and try to improve in the areas I mentioned before: playing with my shoulders to the goal and linking up with my teammates.”

Frosinone are arguably the biggest surprise in Serie A this season, as the newly promoted side sits 6th in the standings, ahead of Juventus and Napoli. Can they aim for something more than survival?

“First, we think about survival, and once we’ve achieved that, we’ll think about something different,” Raimondo concluded.

#1392. ‘Light and sound’ therapy for Alzheimer’s flops in long-anticipated trial

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Asher Mullard is a science journalist based in Ottawa.

The Spectris AD headset produces flashing lights and sounds designed to induce gamma waves in the brain.Credit: Cognito Therapeutics

A device that uses flickering light and rhythmic clicking sounds to stimulate the brain failed to slow memory loss in people with Alzheimer’s disease, according to results from a highly anticipated clinical trial.

The device, called Spectris AD, consists of goggles paired with headphones that individuals wear for an hour a day at home. The flickering light-and-sound show is designed to induce brain activity called gamma waves, which have been linked to increased attention and memory.

But after a year of treatment, participants who used the device did not show any improvement in their cognitive function compared with those assigned to a sham treatment. The results were reported by US medical-technology firm Cognito Therapeutics, which makes the device, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease meeting held in Boston, Massachusetts, on 16 November.

Although disappointed by the results, Christian Howell, Cognito’s chief executive, said that the results show beneficial signs for people with mild cognitive impairment. The company plans to file for approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) next year, he adds.

“The effect that we saw in the mild subgroup was so meaningful,” Howell said. “It just gives us optimism as we move forwards.”

But researchers are not convinced. “The trial was negative,” says Eric McDade, a neurologist at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. “If anything is going to happen after this, it should be a follow-up study in that mild population,” he says.

In the trial, 673 people with Alzheimer’s disease were randomly assigned to use either an active or a sham Spectris AD device for 60 minutes a day for 12 months. After the year, those who used the active device scored, on average, 8.97 points less on a 156-point scale that measured cognition and ability to perform daily activities than they did before using the device. The scores of participants who used the sham device declined by 8.82 points.

Can flashing lights stall Alzheimer’s? What the science shows

Can flashing lights stall Alzheimer’s? What the science shows

Howell says that the device was more effective in people with mild, rather than moderate, cognitive impairment. In the mild-impairment group, active-device users experienced 42% slower decline than sham-device users — a difference of three points on average.

For Rob Howard, a psychiatrist at University College London who specializes in dementia, these data are exploratory rather than a persuasive proof of efficacy.

“If this was a drug, such a clear failure would mean that a company would not proceed to seek regulatory approval,” says Howard. The safety of the device doesn’t make it any more useful to patients, he adds.

Previous trials of Spectris AD haven’t panned out either, adds Howard. In 2024, a smaller trial of the device failed to slow the decline of cognitive and functional abilities in people with Alzheimer’s disease1.

The results are a setback for researchers who have been working to understand how gamma brain-wave modulation could bolster brain health.

#1391. 'One to Watch' - Ben Jacobs: Man Utd Could Move to Sign Gusto for Pochettino

Manchester United could potentially be one of the busiest clubs in the January transfer window as they look to give new manager Mauricio Pochettino what he needs to turn the club's season around, with GIVEMESPORT senior correspondent Ben Jacobs naming a France international as one possible target.

Hopes were high of another strong season for Man United under the permanent leadership of Michael Carrick after their rise up the Premier League table in the first half of 2026, but instead they have made a miserable start to the campaign.

The Red Devils have won just one of their opening 10 Premier League matches this term, while losing three of their five fixtures in the EFL Cup and Champions League too, which has left them in the relegation places in the top flight.

It could get even worse for them this weekend, as they could be bottom of the table by the time they kick off in Pochettino's first match against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday afternoon.

That will happen if Crystal Palace win in Thomas Frank's first game in charge against Coventry City, and Sunderland draw with Aston Villa.

Pochettino knows he has a big task ahead to turn United's fortunes around, and especially from a defensive point of view, where they have conceded four goals against Como and Aston Villa, and three against Bournemouth, in their previous five fixtures.

GIVEMESPORT sources have revealed that club chiefs will look at signing a new striker in January, with Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin one player they are keen on, although the England international looks likely to sign a new contract at Elland Road instead.

Meanwhile, in his latest GMS newsletter, Jacobs has confirmed that United are also looking at the centre-back and full-back positions, with Chelsea's Malo Gusto 'one to watch'.

On the right hand side, even though maybe a right-sided full-back is not as high a priority as a left-sided one, Malo Gusto could be one to watch.

"There’s been no contact between Manchester United and Gusto yet, and Manchester City have looked in the past as well. But Chelsea are prepared to sell at the right price.

“Over the summer, that number was £75million and it would have to be dropped significantly, you would imagine anyway, if anyone’s going to come in for the France International, but more broadly, Gusto’s future is one to watch in this January window."

While United may not want to pay £75m to sign Gusto, especially given Chelsea are willing to sell him if the price is right, a move for the 23-year-old would also make a lot of sense.

The France international has already played under Pochettino, with the duo together at Stamford Bridge from the summer of 2023 to when the Argentine was sacked in May 2024.

Gusto knows how the 54-year-old wants to play and should be able to make an immediate impact in a Pochettino team as a result, while he also boasts 100 Premier League appearances and Champions League experience too.

Most impressive though is Gusto's versatility, as while his primary position is as a right-back or right wing-back, he has also been used as a left-back and even in midfield during his career.

It's no secret that United were looking for left-back competition for Luke Shaw in the summer, having shown strong interest in Newcastle United's Lewis Hall and Barcelona's Alejandro Balde, although neither move materialised as they prioritised signing three central midfielders.

Signing Gusto could kill two birds with one stone if he is seen as a player who can perform well in both roles, although there will of course be some caution given Diogo Dalot is a player who can play left-back and right-back, but has largely ultimately struggled when deployed on his weaker side.

Gusto has 17 caps for France and a big future ahead, and if United were able to secure him for a lower fee than the summer asking price, it could be a smart addition to help Pochettino.

#1390. Striker Che Adams says Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli is big on the small details... 'he loves his FaceTime calls'

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026

No matter how history judges his time in charge of Scotland, no one will ever accuse Sebastien Pocognoli of leaving a single stone unturned.

Intense, intelligent and highly demanding, the Belgian has already shown himself to be big on the small things which can combine to make a significant difference.

Che Adams discovered this for himself in September, even though an injury prevented him from being part of the new man’s first get together in La Manga.

‘I heard from the manager the last time when I wasn’t in the camp,’ he revealed.

‘He loves a FaceTime call. I think he’s taken a few of the boys by surprise when they’ve been out walking their dogs and stuff. I think KT (Kieran Tierney) was out for a walk when he phoned him.

‘He just calls out of the blue and has done it to a few of the boys. It’s unexpected and it’s different because we’ve never experienced something like that. But it’s good.

Che Adams' appearance against North Macedonia was his first under Sebastien Pocognoli

Striker Adams says Pocognoli is more intense than his predecessor and is 'with the times'

John McGinn is within six goals of the scoring record shared by Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law

‘In the last camp when I was out injured, he was on asking how my injury was, how long I’d be out for and if I still wanted to be part of it.

‘The camps haven’t changed much, but the manager is definitely more intense. I think it’s the European style of play and thinking. It’s going to take time for him to understand the boys, understand us as players and understand us as a squad.

‘But he’s really bought into it and wants to help us do well.’

Hang on a minute. A manager who’s more intense than Steve Clarke? You could be forgiven for thinking that’s simply not possible. But Adams feels it is very much the case.

‘With Steve you could have a laugh and you can do that with this gaffer as well,’ he explained.

‘But he’s a lot more intense in terms of detail off the pitch telling you where to be and what to do.

‘This gaffer has good ideas, a good approach to the game.

‘He is with the times, really. Everyone’s buying into it and I definitely think we’ll see the benefits.’

John McGinn believes it could be as long as 18 months before it all comes up roses. But, in football, you rarely get that long.

Starting in St Gallen tomorrow, the Belgian could do with some green shoots emerging.

‘He’s a few years younger (than Clarke) and has a different philosophy on how he wants his team to play,’ added Adams.

‘It just takes time to click, but it’s up to us as players now to show we can do what he wants.

‘We have been together for a number of years now, so we know each other’s games.

‘You could see on Friday us starting to put the manager’s things in practice. We won a lot of balls high with our pressing.

‘He said to us after the game that it’s about the killer moments and we probably didn’t capitalise on them enough. But it was a win and the first one for the gaffer at Hampden.

‘For every manager they need time, but you saw spells there where the movements and patterns of play were very good.

‘It was very important to get the win and build up the confidence.

‘You’ve also got to keep in context things like that it was Luke Graham’s first start for us, but he had the confidence to play those passes in the build-up.

‘So, you have to credit the manager for putting the belief in the young players who have come in as well.’

The comfort for Pocognoli throughout a time of transition is that he can still depend on the old stagers who were central to the success under his predecessor.

On the night when Andy Robertson joined Kenny Dalglish on 102 caps, McGinn claimed a double to put himself within six goals of the scoring record jointly held by Dalglish and Denis Law.

Having just turned 32, there is every chance that the Aston Villa captain can soon claim his own slice of history.

‘It’s amazing for John, he’s such a great person and he deserves it,’ said Adams.

‘Everyone can see what he’s done for club and country, he puts his heart on his sleeve and gives everything.

‘It’s a pleasure to play with him. I really hope he does do it - and I think he will.

‘Everyone is so pleased for him, he’s the best person I’ve met in football. When I came into the squad I didn’t think we’d have people who would achieve these kind of things.

‘I have loved every single minute of it. We have done some great things here.

‘We have been to three major tournaments now, people are making personal achievements as well. But as a team and as a squad it’s about taking that next step now in tournaments.

‘It’s a pleasure to play with these boys. They’re legends of football.’

#1389. Conte vs. Spalletti: The financial gap behind Napoli’s success

Both Antonio Conte and Luciano Spalletti delivered a Scudetto to Napoli, yet the club’s spending and operating costs rose dramatically under the Lecce-born tactician.

La Gazzetta dello Sport has compared Napoli’s transfer spending over the last four seasons: two under Spalletti and two under Conte.

The Partenopei invested €367m during the Conte era: €152m in the 2024-25 season and another €215m in 2025-26. Player sales only partially offset those figures, generating €223m overall and leaving the club with a net transfer deficit of €144m.

The heavy transfer spending left its mark on the club’s finances. Wage costs rose to €142m in 2024-25 and €172m in 2025-26, with amortisation expenses going from €111m to €128m.

As a result, the combined cost of wages and amortisation reached €253m in 2024-25 and climbed to €300m in 2025-26. In practical terms, these costs absorbed 87% and 78% of Napoli’s revenue in Conte’s two seasons.

Luciano Spalletti’s era, which brought the first Scudetto since Diego Armando Maradona, was built on a more restrained financial model. During the Tuscan’s two-year spell, the transfer spending totalled €109m, while player sales generated €91m.

Combined wage and amortisation costs never exceeded €200m during the Spalletti era.

The gap is evident in performance as well. Although both coaches won one Serie A title, each Serie A point in the Spalletti era cost Napoli €2.3m compared to €3.5m under Conte.

Napoli’s biggest stars during the Spalletti era, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Victor Osimhen, were sold when Conte was in charge for €80m and €75m, respectively. Kvara played only six months under Conte, while Osimhen never featured under the Lecce-born coach, but their sales proved crucial in financing transfers over the last two seasons.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

Although Spalletti is clearly a nobody now, Conte has lost his marbles a long time back.

Conte is the same guy who made the ridiculous “You can’t eat at a 100€ restaurant with only 10€ in your pocket” remark, only to famously suck at other huge spenders like Chelsea, Shinter, Tottenham etc. and finally going on to make Napoli spend like 300€ to get them a plate of Spaghetti alla Carbonara and 1 glass of Limoncello.

#1388. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

News breaks that City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.

Telegraph Sport understands that Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur were contacted in advance of the email to the other 15 clubs.

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

#1387. Le Tissier Tipped Him As Southampton's Next Lallana, Now He Plays Non-League Football

In the last 50 years, Southampton are widely recognised as having one of the best academies in football.

From bringing through the likes of Matthew Le Tissier and Alan Shearer in the 1980s, to Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and James Ward-Prowse in more recent years, Southampton have made a lot of money through player sales.

As well as Le Tissier and Shearer, considered to be two of the greatest Premier League players of all time, Gareth Bale and Theo Walcott are two more players from the academy who went on to play at the highest level for Real Madrid and Arsenal.

Luke Shaw was another who came through the ranks before joining Manchester United, where he still is 13 years later, and Calum Chambers was another who left St Mary's for Arsenal after breaking through under Mauricio Pochettino.

It's fair to say that those success stories have dried up a little in more recent years, while the club has spent more time battling at the bottom of the Premier League and in the Championship, with a number of players failing to make the grade having made first-team appearances.

Striker Sam Gallagher left for Blackburn Rovers in 2019, Matt Targett joined Aston Villa after a 15-year association with the south coast outfit, while Harrison Reed signed for Fulham after failing to break into the midfield at St Mary's.

Two of the more recent rare success stories are Tyler Dibling, who joined Everton for a huge fee in the summer of 2025, and Jimmy-Jay Morgan, who is currently scoring for fun at West Bromwich Albion after leaving Saints for Chelsea as a 17-year-old.

Southampton have had other young players who looked on course for a big future at St Mary's too, especially following their U21 Premier League Cup win against Blackburn in 2015.

After watching the final live, Saints legend Le Tissier was asked by Sky Sports to pick out five youngsters to watch who had first-team potential, and he selected Gallagher, Targett, Reed and Sam McQueen.

Le Tissier was particularly complimentary about his final pick, Jake Hesketh, who joined Saints' academy at the age of 10 having been born in Stockport.

He reminds me of Adam Lallana in the way he plays. He's got good feet, moves with the ball really well, and is very, very natural.

"However, he's got a bit of growing and strengthening to do and it won't be an instant thing for him to break through to senior level."

It turned out that Le Tissier may have been right, about his warning over Hesketh.

The teenager was actually promoted to the first-team by Ronald Koeman during the 2014-15 season because of injury issues, and he made his debut for the club in a 2-1 home defeat to Manchester United in December.

Hesketh made a further top flight appearance against Burnley, but he then fell back down the pecking order until Claude Puel was appointed as Koeman's successor in 2016.

He made two further appearances under the Frenchman, scoring his first senior goal in a League Cup tie against Crystal Palace in September 2016, and he also played in the Europa League tie away against Hapoel Be'er Sheva.

The attacking midfielder then picked up an injury and even though he signed a new four-and-a-half year contract in December 2016, he never wore the Southampton shirt again.

He spent time on loan at Burton Albion, MK Dons, Lincoln City and Crawley Town, before leaving St Mary's on a permanent basis for Eastleigh in 2021 after 17 years with the club.

Following two seasons with the National League outfit, Hesketh remained in the Southampton area when he joined Southern League Premier Division club Sholing FC, where he still plays to this day.as a 30-year-old.

#1386. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli admits his newlook team need to deliver sooner rather than later

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.

Appointed Steve Clarke’s successor in the summer, the Belgian’s attempts to bring in fresh faces and a new style of play has produced mixed results in his opening five Nations League games.

Following Friday’s win over North Macedonia, John McGinn warned the Tartan Army that it could take as long as 18 months for everything to click into place.

But ahead of the final group match in St Gallen tomorrow evening, the manager acknowledged it’s incumbent on him to accelerate that time frame.

Asked if he felt he had to deliver sooner, he said: ‘Yeah, for sure, but we’re only talking about 18 months because John said that. He could have said 15 months. I don’t know. But, for sure, it needs to be quicker.

‘In 18 months, it will be the time of the Euros and that is what he meant. We have to go there and be prepared for this in 18 months’ time.

Sebastien Pocognoli  says his Scotland team need to show progress 'game after game'

‘For sure, game after game, we need to see improvement.

‘Some new faces will come back in March. So, step by step we will have more ideas and in one month’s time a lot can change also.’

McGinn also said that the players were fully behind the manager, reiterating the point previously made by Andy Robertson and Scott McTominay.

‘I can tell you that in the time we have had together the players have been doing well in terms of replicating what I ask them to do,’ the manager stressed.

‘They know that and that’s the most important part.

‘They buy in. They like it. I think they enjoy it too. You can see when players don’t enjoy it.

‘For sure, when you win it’s more enjoyable, but it would be very bad if they weren’t enjoying it and we were also not winning games.

‘So, right now I think we are working well. We give special attention to the collective.

‘In all the camps, I am very clear about what I expect on the pitch. The players wanted this when I arrived. They wanted clarity. And I think that’s what I have tried to bring.’

To claim second place in the group, Scotland need to defeat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t win in North Macedonia.

That outcome would ensure that Pocognoli’s men would be a pot two side in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Asked what it would take to pull off what would be a stunning win in St Gallen, the manager said: ‘Let’s be brave, but be intelligent.

‘It’s about mentality. They (Switzerland) are a very good team, so we need to be smart. Sometimes they will go through our lines with a low block or a high block as they have the quality.

‘We will try to be intense and strong in the duel because I think that’s the first piece to have a good game.’

Pocognoli’s side were booed off at half-time on Friday with criticism of the performance persisting despite them going on to win the game.

But the manager claims he’s oblivious to wider concerns about the performances to date, saying: ‘No, I’m not aware of this. That’s why I was surprised (at the question).

John McGinn suggested that it could take 18 months for Scotland to click under Pocognoli

‘Yes, there were some boos at half-time. I think that’s part of it, it’s been like this for years.

‘I know we are colleagues, but I’m not reading the press.

‘So, I’m not aware of the criticism. I just want to make the supporters happy.

‘If they aren’t yet happy, we will try to do better.

‘There’s pressure in all the jobs with a club. It can be external, it can be internal. It is part of the job.

‘I’m very self-critical about myself. So, that’s the first thing. Try to be stable when we win, when we lose.

‘I’m always thinking what we can do better. If there’s some criticism, that’s fine.

‘But there there were also a lot of positives after the North Macedonia game.

‘I was the first one to say calm down as we need to see more.’

#1385. JJ Gabriel: Spanish Media Cast Strong Verdict on Man Utd Youngster

JJ Gabriel hasn't even kicked a ball for any of Real Madrid's teams yet and the former Manchester United starlet has already made an impression on Spanish media.

The 16-year-old stunned United when he asked to leave the club in September, and he became the most in-demand teenage talent in the months that followed. As soon as the news dropped that he wanted out of Old Trafford without even making a senior appearance, the likes of Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Chelsea and Manchester City were all linked.

Madrid eventually won the race to sign Gabriel, a move still to be completed and one that confused United's fans because of his supposed wish for regular senior football. His family, including his father, are thought to believe he is a similar superstar talent as Lamine Yamal, but he might have to work hard convincing the Spanish media that he's the real deal.

Gabriel bid farewell to United with a social media post this week, confirming his departure with a video that veteran players often use when wishing fans an emotional goodbye after lengthy stays at clubs. Given that the England youngster didn't even feature for the club's first-team, it caused a stir not only at Old Trafford.

Spanish commentator Juanma Castano discussed the video during an appearance on El Partidazo de Cope and he reacted in astonishment. Pointing out a lack of prominence while at United, he said:

"I say this with the slight fear that this kid might go on to become the greatest player of all time. But it’s just unbelievable. This lad hasn’t played a single minute for Manchester United. Yet he’s said goodbye as if he were a United legend."

Castano added: "Someone leaving the club, the sort of player whose departure would have people in Manchester in tears." He explained that Gabriel is just "a 16-year-old kid who hasn’t even made his debut. He’s a prospect."

When Gabriel pushed to leave United, questions arose about his attitude and those advising him at this stage of his career. Jamie Carragher particularly warned about the influence family can have on a youth prospect and demanding too much, too soon.

Castano echoed this when explaining his concerns about Gabriel and his mindset. He believes that the English winger isn't "what he’s being led to believe he is" and that will lead to “difficulties this boy will face, believing he’s already a football star.”

The Spaniard's colleague, Manolo Lama, has partially blamed the media for building Gabriel up as a superstar in the making at the age of 16:

"We in the media are largely to blame for this. Every week, I see young players, 14 or 15-year-olds, at Real Madrid. Some go on to succeed, others don’t. But we almost always attribute far more value to them than they actually possess."

He added: “Just pick up any newspaper. Every day you’ll find a ‘diamond’ from somewhere or a ‘gem’ from somewhere else.”

Gabriel caught the eye throughout his journey through United's youth ranks, putting in dazzling displays that had the UK press believing him to be Carrington's biggest talent in decades. That included handing him the nickname 'Kid Messi' and constantly reporting on his ventures such as his major sponsorship deal with Nike.

United have yet to even confirm Gabriel's exit and, from their perspective, the club did all they could to convince him to stay and sign a new contract. They are frustrated to have lost one of their academy's most exciting teenagers, but there are others whom they hold in high regard.

Take for example, Shea Lacey, who, unlike Gabriel, has broken into the senior team and has already won over fans with cameo appearances. The 19-year-old came off the bench to set Matheus Cunha up in a 3-2 comeback win over AS Roma in the Champions League earlier this month.

The Red Devils don't have to worry about Noah Ajayi's future as the German starlet signed his first long-term professional contract with the club in September. Gabriel got most of the plaudits for the U18's last season but Ajayi was equally important in attack under Darren Fletcher.

Tynan Thompson is another name United will be hoping can fulfill his potential after forking out an initial £4 million to sign the 18-year-old from Tottenham Hotspur. The English winger may well be viewed as Gabriel's like-for-like replacement at youth level and a talent who could step up to the senior level like Ayden Heaven.

United's main concern right now should be about their first-team struggles that have led to the sacking of Michael Carrick. Mauricio Pochettino has replaced him and the Argentine's first match back in the Premier League is a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on Sunday (November 22nd).

#1384. How much Napoli would save by selling De Bruyne in January

Reports in Italy over the last few weeks indicate that Kevin De Bruyne could leave Napoli as early as January, which could provide the Partenopei with around €10m to reinvest if they do allow the Belgian superstar to leave midway through the season.

De Bruyne is into the final year of the two-year contract he signed with Napoli after leaving Manchester City at the end of the 2024-25 season. There is an option to extend that agreement by a further 12 months, until the end of the 2027-28 season, but this appears an unlikely scenario at this stage.

Reports earlier this week claimed that Dutch side PSV Eindhoven are interested in pursuing a deal for De Bruyne, potentially as early as January, and that they are willing to offer around €2m to Napoli for the 35-year-old, who will have less than six months remaining on his contract during the next transfer window.

Some outlets claim that Napoli will hold out for a larger transfer fee, while others, including the Corriere dello Sport, still claim that Napoli wish to keep hold of De Bruyne until the end of the season at least.

There have also been suggestions that De Bruyne is keen on the idea of a move to the Netherlands, as he and his family could move into the home they own in the Belgian province of Limburg, which borders the Netherlands.

According to the latest updates from La Gazzetta dello Sport, what is becoming clear is that De Bruyne would need to take a significant pay cut if he is to join PSV during the January transfer window.

The Pink Paper claims that De Bruyne earns a net salary of around €5m per season with Napoli, which costs the club around €10m per season gross. La Gazzetta dello Sport reports that PSV would not ‘seem able to afford’ these figures.

If Napoli do offload De Bruyne in January, though, they will save half a season’s worth of wages, around €5m gross, plus around €2.5m in bonuses that would no longer be valid, as well as a transfer fee of €2m or above, which could provide Napoli with around €10m to reinvest in January.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1383. Is academia’s risk-averse culture stifling scientific discovery?

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Nessa Carey's career has straddled both academia and industry. “In industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams,” she says.

Academia, on the other hand, is more personality-driven, and feels more individualistic. “Failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal,” she adds.

But as global research collaborations become more multidisciplinary, a culture change is needed in higher education, says Carey, who now runs a training business that supports biotechnology and drug discovery spinoffs.

Earlier this year, Carey spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the penultimate episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Carey urges academia to look at how industry handles failure, where struggling projects are abandoned more quickly.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03772-y

Is innovation as slow as it's often labelled?

Oftentimes we talk about innovation being slow, but in fact, you know, many of us feel like we're living in an ever-changing society.

After the failure and innovation session, the chair, Dr Nejra van Zalk, a design psychologist at Imperial College London, reported back to delegates attending the Failure in Science Conference, held in April this year.

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

Why do we choose innovation in one area of healthcare, for example, and not in another area? And who makes those decisions?

Why do we focus on obesity drugs and pump money into that, rather than helping to fix musculoskeletal issues in children who would have much better outcomes over a lifetime.

I'm Dr Stephen Webster, director of The Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don't.

And in episode five of this series, we explore the business of discovery.

To put it bluntly, when it comes to failure, could universities learn a thing or two from industry?

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

How can we safely incorporate failure into our working models?

Can we look to industry to see how they're doing it when they actually, they cut their losses sooner and they abandon projects quicker and they can quantify their risks in different ways than we can in academia.

So my name is Nessa Carey, I'm a PhD scientist. And I've worked in academia, in industry, and as a freelancer. So I've kind of done a lot of things over the space of my career.

Oh, so so many failures. I started out with the classic academic failures of having grants rejected, having papers rejected.

In industry, you get things like programmes that you simply can't keep running. And also if you move to industry, you will be made redundant at some point or another.

And it's very easy, particularly the first time, to view that as a personal failure, but as you get more experienced, you realize it's just about organizations, it's just about shifting priorities, and actually it's not that big a deal.

So your definition of failure changes as your career changes. And also as you get older, I think it changes as well.

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

I wanted to ask us, and perhaps ask the panel: as society, and this is not simply a UK perspective I don't think, have we become hyper risk averse?

Is that the direction that we're heading in?

And if so, where is the space for failure, and particularly the space for failure in science?

So, in the opening session of the conference at Imperial College, Professor Jem Woods suggested that we have become too risk averse and that that has really negative consequences, for example in academia.

And I think I absolutely agree with that, but I don't think it's just academia that is negatively impacted by this.

And I think the conversation has shifted, and not necessarily in a way that's helpful. And I think it's particularly a lot of pressure on younger people.

So I do quite a lot of outreach work in schools, and I see young students who are under enormous pressure to do well at their GCSEs or their A levels or whatever is the equivalent in another country, because they have to get onto the right course at the right college. They have to get a career trajectory that's working in the right direction.

And so I think there's a much bigger fear of failure because the stakes have been made artificially high.

In reality, as long as you do a course that you're happy on at a university where you're happy living, you'll do fine.

But we've built in this terrible sequential success demand on the young, and I think it's also exacerbated by [the fact we] we now have much more public discourse because we have social media, and everybody posts their triumphs. Everybody posts their success. You look at LinkedIn, and it's just full of people celebrating their promotion, their latest certificate, etc.

The trouble is that's not real. That's not how life generally progresses. You try stuff, you stuff up, you learn from it, and you move on.

And if we always class that as failure rather than a normal part of learning, then I think we do create really, really big problems for the future because everybody will try and stay inside their comfort zone.

Everybody will be frightened of doing something wrong.

It's a big problem in science because science thrives on innovation, but it's a big problem in any creative sector, and we run the risk of situations where people would rather do nothing than take a risk.

And you see that in organizations as well, and that's a really big problem.

I think what academia could do with learning from industry in terms of failure is to depersonalize it somewhat.

I think that's extremely difficult to do in reality.

One of the things that I enjoyed about working in industry, as opposed to working in academia, is in industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams. And yes, you may be the leader of a team, but you're still a team.

Academia, I find generally is much more individualistic.

If you have a much more individualistic environment, it is much harder to acknowledge failure as being simply a consequence of good decisions that are made by a team.

In academia, failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal. And it's very personal, in particular, to the Principal Investigators.

In industry, you can be doing really interesting work on a project, and then you do the killer experiment and realize your project can't go anywhere. And as a team, and as the leader of a team, you make the decision that that project needs to be terminated.

Now, that in academia would feel like failure because you can't then go on and apply for grants for it.

In industry, there's much more an emphasis in good companies on “did we make the right decision?”, and if you made the right decision, then the target failed or the program failed, but you didn't necessarily fail as an individual.

And I think it's that difference between viewing things as projects and teams and viewing things as individual endeavours.

And given that more and more science is becoming multidisciplinary, multi-team, it would make so much more sense if academia could start to change its culture towards that, because on the whole, the big papers that we see coming out now – they're big team efforts, and yet reward still tends to remain very individual.

So it's a structural issue. It's not just about people.

I think academia could adapt well by adopting some of the good managerial and people development skills of industry.

Academia is, in my experience, much more driven by personalities, and that creates enormous emotional heft behind things.

In industry, of course, there are big personalities. There are in every sector, but because you're working as an organization, you don't have quite this same strange mix of your personal emotional life with your professional life, and so you can fail professionally without it having quite the same impact on you as an individual emotionally, if that makes sense.

Something that the industry has got very, very good on is identifying killer experiments, carrying them out, and doing the thing that is considered a cliche now – but is absolutely critical – of fail fast, fail quickly, fail early, fail cheaply: that you don't keep trying to progress something that cannot get to the end point that you need.

And I think industry, on the whole, is very good at that. It used to be very bad. It's got better.

Academia is terrible at that in my experience, in that what will happen is somebody has their favourite target, their favourite process, their favourite enzyme, and they just keep working on it because they have a reputation for that and because they can keep working on it, rather than thinking “do you know what? It'd be really good to set up this experiment, see if I'm on the right track, and if I'm not, I'll kill it.” Instead, what they tend to do is just find other things they can keep working on in the same field.

Now, sometimes that's entirely appropriate, and sometimes it's that real curiosity-led stuff that takes us in a weird direction and opens up all sorts of things.

But there is always a risk that you will just keep chugging away at something because you know you'll at least get a couple of papers out of it, or because your PhD student needs the data for their thesis, etc.

It's a very different environment, and so it's not that I'm saying we should import everything from industry into academia, but I do think sometimes academia could benefit from the critical thinking of industry that goes: take away the emotion and actually look at this from scratch and say, “would we carry on if we were starting now?”

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

So I mentioned these grand challenges; We often talk about them in science circles, The grand challenges. What's the role of science in helping society address these grand challenges?

And the emergence of innovation in technologies, I think has now switched to hyper disruptive technologies, and that's specifically around how we manage, or [how] information is managed. (When I say we, maybe it's not managed).

And then societal and community and individual access to those innovations in technology, and I think it's often labelled as ‘The BBC's Post-Truth Society’, because there were many of the BBC journalists (and some of them may be in the audience I don't know) who talked a lot about this emergence of that technological system in the post-truth society. And we have real questions in science to answer around that understanding of the way that information is generated and the way it's perceived and used societally.

So, in the opening session, Jem Woods was talking about the fact that there's been a drop of trust in science, and I wouldn't say it's just science.

There's a drop in trust in multiple areas, including in our trust in politicians, and our trust in writers, and our trust in the media.

And I think it's phenomenally important that scientists continue to do their work to the highest level of probity, and the vast majority of scientists do that, and that is true whatever sector you're in.

Scientists are remarkably similar, whether they're in academia or they're in industry; they're there because they want to do good science.

I think it's vital that everybody continues to do really good science. I think it's also vital, though, that we do challenge one another appropriately and professionally.

But what is also really important is that scientists continue to communicate, to a wider public, what is important about science and the scientific method, and also to be very upfront about the limitations of our research and the limitations of our findings.

This again, I think, ties into the issue of success and failure, because one of the things that's happened is public engagement and communication of science have been added to the academic workload.

The academic workload never decreases; new stuff always gets added to it, and it becomes another box to tick.

And there is a risk that people not only need to do good science, but they need to do science that can be communicated well.

And I think the most dangerous thing for academia is that it's constantly under pressure to justify why its science is being done. What is the benefit, the direct, very tangible benefit for humanity?

And that creates pressure to overstate one's outcomes, to be too black and white about it because black and white stories sell – it's much easier to sell a black and white story – but we have to be really careful not to do that because every time we do that and get challenged, we undermine the faith not so much in our science, because each member of the public has probably forgotten us, but the faith in science itself.

We shouldn't be scared of saying it's complicated, and so I think there is a real risk there that by being unsubtle about how we communicate our science, we actually undermine faith in a field which has essentially added enormous benefit to humanity and to the planet, and we need to be very careful not to lose that.

So I've worked in the field of innovation for about 25 years, and it's just as difficult now as it was 25 years ago.

But I think there are particular issues now that we're facing as a world that we didn't face back then. AI is the obvious one of having created a technology that actually may outrun us, and no one's quite clear how that's going to play out now.

But I think there are bigger issues at stake here as well.

I think it's very difficult when so much science is being published and being done to work out which of it genuinely has the potential to shift the needle on a particular issue.

But I think it's actually at risk of us having such a focus on innovation, in the sense of ‘where's the next great widget? Where's the next great drug?’, that we forget that technological innovation may not actually be what we require to solve particular problems.

So one of the things that really really frustrates me is seeing more and more emphasis, and more and more funding, in climate change going into carbon capture.

Carbon capture at scale is an entirely unproven technology, and it's not clear at all that it can solve the climate change problem.

We do, however, know that moving to electric cars makes a huge difference, and yet we are not in the UK legislating to do that appropriately.

We also have a situation where drug companies are spending billions of dollars to develop drugs for chronic health conditions that we actually know are caused essentially by social inequality and poverty.

We would be so much better as societies if we would put our money into more equitable healthcare systems, more equitable food availability systems.

We would have an enormous return on investment, but we don't see that return on investment for a very long time, and it's not a capitalist return on investment, it's a government return on investment.

So my concern is that our biggest failures will come because we constantly try to ‘tech’ our way out of problems that don't actually require technological solutions.

They require different, longer-term, less glossy solutions that don't make money for companies, and our systems on the whole run in a way that have placed an awful lot of, say, healthcare and environmental responsibilities and opportunities on big capitalist companies, when actually they are not the right structure to deliver those outcomes.

So that is where I think our biggest failures will come: We will ‘tech’ when we shouldn't be ‘tech-ing’. We will try and ‘tech’ very expensively when actually we could have made smaller investments with much more impact.

And it is deeply frustrating to me that also we as scientists will go “don't worry, we'll come up with a technological solution.” instead of saying “we may never come up with a technological solution, but if you talk to our friends in the social sciences, they already know what needs to be done. Why on earth aren't you doing this?” And that, I think, is a failure on the part of science to pretend that we are the ones who will solve everything.

#1381. Ryan Giggs Named Two British Stadiums With the Best Atmospheres He’s Seen

No player in the history of the Premier League has made more appearances for Manchester United than Ryan Giggs and he 'won the lot' as their proud Stretford End so eloquently put it.

During Giggs' legendary career, he became the most decorated footballer not only to wear a United shirt but also in English football. The Welshman got his hands on 34 major trophies, 13 league titles and was part of the team that won the treble in 1999.

The unfortunate thing about time in football is that the heroes of yesteryear are quickly forgotten, and the younger generation certainly don't seem to realise just how incredibly talented Giggs was. Most weren't even alive when he glided his way through Arsenal at Highbury to score the most famous FA Cup goal in history and many may have even missed his exploits in Moscow against Chelsea in 2008.

Giggs carved out a career only one can dream of and that meant travelling the globe to play against the very best teams on the planet. He experienced some of the most hostile crowds in world football but the atmosphere at two stadiums particularly left their mark on him.

Giggs played in some of the most heated rivalries in British football, including feisty clashes with Liverpool at Anfield. As enthralling as those fixtures can be, they pale in comparison to the derby between Celtic and Rangers.

Back in 2018, Giggs admitted that he wished to have sampled the atmosphere of an Old Firm Derby having spent his entire career at Old Trafford. Speaking to the Daily Record, he said: "I was talking to Declan John last year about coming up for the Old Firm but he has gone now. It’s something I’ve always wanted to experience."

Giggs added: "There’s no Welsh players in Scotland at the moment unfortunately but it’s something I am definitely keen to do. I’ll get there at some point because everyone I speak to who has been there says it’s unreal. I have played in Glasgow."

The former United winger played seven times against Celtic and Rangers in Champions League competition, stepping out on the Ibrox and Parkhead pitches. Those outings seemed to whet his appetite to attend a derby game:

"Those were amazing atmospheres, probably up there with the best atmospheres I played in."

Giggs even recalled a trip to Turkey but insisted Glasgow was in a league of its own: "I remember going to Turkey in the early days against Galatasaray and it was ferocious but going to Glasgow surpassed that for intensity. I played at Ibrox in the Champions League when Phil Neville scored and a couple of times against Celtic."

He added: "We drew one and lost one. I managed to score in the draw. The noise was incredible. When that Champions League music went on and the crowd got behind the team, it was amazing. You didn’t just have to face 11 men, you had to face those passionate crowds as well."

Giggs's former United teammate Wayne Rooney not only wanted to taste an Old Firm Derby but to do so as a Celtic player. The former England striker revealed he had wished to have played for the Bhoys at some stage of his career.

When Giggs hung up his boots in May 2014, he didn't step into punditry like many of his former teammates nor did he leave Old Trafford. He instead took up an assistant coaching role, first as a player-manager in David Moyes' team before taking charge as caretaker manager and eventually assisting Louis van Gaal.

Some expected him to become permanent boss but instead he's watched Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and Michael Carrick try their luck in the dugout. He did, however, land the Wales national team job, spending four years in the role before resigning in 2022.

Giggs' personal life has meant he hasn't been back in football management since, but before he managed his country, he landed on Celtic's radar. In 2016, the Scottish club were looking to replace Ronny Delia and the Welshman was a shock name added to their managerial shortlist.

The Manchester United legend named one famous British stadium as having the best atmosphere he ever experienced as a player.

That came while he assisted Van Gaal and The Daily Mail claim that he had reservations about moving to Scotland. If he had decided to take charge at Parkhead, he'd have been able to experience the Old Firm Derby as a manager, potentially even coming up against his former Liverpool foe Steven Gerrard, who became Rangers boss two years' later.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
