a, Characteristics of the two studies. b, Test–retest ICC(2,1) for bilateral, left and right regional volumes (two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measurement). Points are ICC estimates. Bars show 95% confidence intervals computed by irr::icc. n = 8 independent participants, each scanned twice (16 scans, paired measurements). Red indicates ICC < 0.4. c, Pearson correlation heatmap of hypothalamic structure volumes and age at MRI in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants (n = 165 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across all pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). d, Age–volume Pearson r in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants, analysed as pooled (black, n = 165), CBA (orange, n = 91) and AMBR (blue, n = 74) samples. Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across 26 age–volume correlations per analysis. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05, open circles non-significance. e, Associations of age, female sex and intracranial volume with subregion volumes in AMBR, CBA and pooled participants. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients. Bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × s.e.). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in pooled models. Two-sided t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. BH correction covered 26 regions per predictor and cohort. Exact estimates, intervals, t statistics, degrees of freedom and raw/adjusted P are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of extrahypothalamic volumes and age at MRI (n = 458 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across unique pairwise correlations within the matrix (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson correlations in the pooled cohort (n = 458 independent participants), CBA (n = 256) and AMBR (n = 202). Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across all 26 regional age–volume correlations within each cohort. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05. Open circles indicate adjusted P ≥ 0.05. c, Forest plots of Gaussian GLM coefficients for hypothalamic (top) and extrahypothalamic (bottom) volumes, ordered by coefficient estimate. Points show fitted coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 316 independent participants in every model, with covariates as in Fig. 1c. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 308 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all eight coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Point color and size indicate adjusted significance. d, Age, female sex and intracranial volume coefficients for extrahypothalamic structures. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in the pooled analysis. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. P values were BH-adjusted across 26 regions separately for each predictor and cohort. e, Body mass index (BMI) associations in AMBR-only Gaussian GLMs. Points show BMI coefficients per SD of BMI and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 174 independent participants in each regional model. Models adjusted for age, sex, cognition, amyloid status, cognition × amyloid status, HbA1c, Epworth sleepiness score and intracranial volume. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 164 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all ten model coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Exact results for all panels are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, PCA of 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structure volumes (n = 458 participants). Scatter plots are colored by eight covariates: age, sex, amyloid-β status, cognitive status, intracranial volume (ICV), total brain volume (TBV), study and amyloid days. Three variants are shown: raw volumes (top, PC1 = 44.2%, PC2 = 14.4%), fully residualized for age, sex, ICV, TBV and study (middle, PC1 = 27.6%, PC2 = 13.1%), and partially residualized for sex, ICV, TBV and study (bottom, PC1 = 27.4%, PC2 = 13.9%). b–c, PC1 and PC2 loadings from raw (b) and fully residualized (c) PCA. Bars are red for negative loadings and teal for positive loadings. d, Changes in PC1 (left) and PC2 (right) loadings from raw (orange) to fully residualized (green) PCA, shown as dumbbell plots ordered by magnitude of change. e, Associations of PC1–PC5 scores with nine covariates in raw and partially residualized PCA. Continuous covariates were tested using two-sided Pearson correlations, with r2 as effect size. Categorical covariates were tested using omnibus one-way ANOVA F-tests, with η2 as effect size and an upper-tail F reference distribution. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted across 45 PC–covariate tests separately for each PCA variant. n = 458 participants, with data available for cognitive status in 422, amyloid-β status in 340, CogDays in 441 and AmyloidDays in 358. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. f, Regional volume versus age in n = 181 independent male participants. Each point represents one participant, colored by combined cognitive and amyloid status (black, missing status). Black LOESS curves estimate conditional mean volume. Shading shows pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the fitted curves, rather than between-participant standard deviations. g, Regional volume distributions after nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching of AD and cognitively unimpaired, amyloid-negative participants on sex and age. The pooled comparison includes 24 AD participants (18 men, 6 women) and 24 matched controls (16 men, 8 women). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Dots represent individual participants, including observations beyond the whiskers. Duplicate outlier symbols are suppressed. h, ROC curves from class-balanced logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation, using 13 hypothalamic subregion volumes or total hypothalamic volume to predict cognitive impairment (n = 422 participants, 140 impaired, 282 unimpaired), amyloid positivity (n = 340, 63 positive, 277 negative) and AD status (n = 316, 24 AD, 292 others). AUCs are mean ± standard deviation across five folds. The subregion model had a higher mean AUC for all three outcomes. No formal comparison was performed. i, Univariate ROC curves predicting AD status from 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures and total hypothalamic volume (n = 316 participants, 24 AD, 292 others), sorted by descending AUC. The arcuate nucleus (AN; ARC in the main text), fornix (fx), paraventricular nucleus (Pa) and ventromedial nucleus (VM) were the strongest predictors. When lower volume predicted AD (indicated by “−”), scores were sign-inverted before ROC calculation.

a, Donor metadata. The table summarizes condition, age, Braak stage, APOE genotype, amyloid-β status, postmortem delay (PMD), RNA integrity number (RIN) and time of death for each donor. Accompanying heatmaps show donors clustered by pathology metrics (left) and quality metrics (right), with annotation bars indicating condition, time of death, pathology and quality. b, UMAP showing nuclei from this study embedded within a reference atlas of 25 million publicly available human brain cells, colored by major cell type and condition. c, UMAP of the integrated dataset following scVI batch correction, with nuclei colored by condition, batch, individual, and inclusion of the Siletti et al. dataset. d, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean number of genes detected per nucleus, stratified by cell type and condition. Each tissue sample is one hypothalamic subregion from one donor. The center line is the median, box bounds are the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Observations beyond the whiskers are shown as points. CTL and AD contain seven donors each (AD includes the familial case). Young reference samples derive from three donors, except young epithelial cells, which derive from one donor. In cell-type order neuron, epithelial, endothelial, ependymal, OPC, astrocyte, fibroblast, oligodendrocyte, microglia, and leukocyte, n (CTL/AD/young tissue samples) is 21/21/24, 8/4/2, 21/21/19, 19/17/19, 21/21/24, 21/21/24, 21/21/23, 21/21/24, 21/21/22 and 21/21/19. The epithelial samples come from four CTL and three AD donors. These are descriptive summaries, and no inferential test is shown. e, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean UMI count per nucleus, with the same samples and group sizes as d. Boxplot elements are as in d. The y-axis is logarithmic. No inferential comparison is presented. f, Stacked bar plots showing cell-type composition for samples from each hypothalamic subregion (SCN, MN, and ARC). g, Bar plot quantifying the total number of nuclei for each cell type in the final dataset.

Selected significantly enriched Hallmark (top) and Gene Ontology biological process (GO:BP; bottom) pathways from GSEA. The analysis was performed on genes ranked by their signed model weights. The dot plot shows the top pathways for the all-cell model and for each of the five cell-type-specific models. The x-axis represents the absolute NES, dot size represents the number of genes in a pathway, and color indicates significance (−log10[FDR]).

a, Top row: violin plots displaying significant DEGs across specific major cell types (endothelial cells, microglia, and OPCs) from snRNA-seq, comparing CTL and AD individuals. Bottom row: boxplots illustrating the normalized log2 abundance of the corresponding significant differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in CSF, comparing healthy controls (HC) with AD patients. Statistical significance with BH correction is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). b, UMAP projections illustrating the expression scores for three senescence-related and three NFT-related gene signatures across all nuclei. c, Violin plots comparing the expression scores of three NFT-related signatures across major cell types. Per-sample mean UCell scores for the NFT Orr signature were higher in AD than control (Wilcoxon rank-sum test on 18 AD versus 21 control samples, BH-adjusted across cell types: microglia P = 0.037, OPC P = 0.025). d, Violin plots showing the expression of key senescence-related genes (CDKN1A, canonical; CALR, responses; SOD2, initiators) across major cell types. Pseudobulk edgeR-LRT false discovery rate (FDR) is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). e–f, Module scores for the mTOR signaling (e) and extracellular matrix (ECM; f) gene sets, comparing control and AD donors at the sample level, stratified by cell type. Scores were computed using Seurat’s AddModuleScore (background-corrected mean expression relative to randomly sampled control gene sets matched by expression level). Each point represents the mean per-sample score for a given cell type (minimum 10 cells per sample). Boxes show median and IQR; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. Brackets indicate pairwise comparisons with BH-adjusted significance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

a, Split UMAP embeddings of hypothalamic microglia/macrophage nuclei by group: young, 3,213 nuclei (3 donors), CTL, 24,648 (7 donors), AD, 20,087 (6 donors), and AD_44, 3,472 (1 donor), totaling 51,420 nuclei. In each panel, the full population is shown in light gray and the indicated group is overlaid, colored by inferred pseudotime (top), group identity (middle) or local nuclear density (2D kernel density estimate, bottom). Young nuclei occupy a discrete low-pseudotime region, whereas AD nuclei are shifted toward high pseudotime. b, Group-specific kernel density estimates of pseudotime, with the pooled distribution shown in gray. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Dashed vertical lines mark mean pseudotime: young 1.50, CTL 2.38, AD 2.90 and AD_44 2.12. The distribution shifts rightward from young to CTL to AD. c, Empirical cumulative distributions of nuclear pseudotime. The maximal vertical separation between AD and CTL is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance D = 0.27, presented as a descriptive effect size. Because nuclei within a donor are not independent, inference used donor-level mean pseudotime: AD versus CTL, 6 versus 7 donors, two-sided exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.0047. Young and AD_44 are shown descriptively and were not tested. d, Group composition of 22 fixed-width pseudotime bins (width 0.2, early to late from left to right). Each bar shows the fraction of nuclei contributed by each group. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and were not tested. The AD fraction increases along pseudotime (Spearman ρ = 0.97, n = 22 bins, two-sided unadjusted P = 1.0 × 10−13), from near-absence in the earliest bins to dominance in the latest bins. A donor-aware binomial mixed model (in-segment versus out, group + (1 | donor), two-sided Wald tests, BH-adjusted across 44 segment × comparison tests) showed AD nuclei were underrepresented relative to CTL in early bins 4–9 (log-OR − 3.23 to −1.28, adjusted P ≤ 0.017) and overrepresented in late bins 16–21 (log-OR +0.62 to +1.31, adjusted P ≤ 0.044), with a single crossover at pseudotime ≈ 2.3–2.9. Exact estimates for every bin are in Supplementary Table 10. e, Nuclear pseudotime by group, with counts as in a. Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Nuclei beyond the whiskers are plotted individually. This panel is descriptive. See c for donor-level inference. f, Top: per-nucleus expression of CSF1R, APOE, B2M and TIMP2 in microglia (same data as Fig. 4f). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Asterisks indicate FDRs from pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD versus CTL, 1 d.f., one pseudobulk per sample, 18 AD samples from 6 donors and 21 CTL samples from 7 donors, BH-adjusted across genes): CSF1R FDR = 3.1 × 10−7 (****). APOE, B2M and TIMP2 were nonsignificant (FDR ≥ 0.05). Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and excluded from these tests. Bottom: CSF protein abundance in young healthy controls (<65 years, n = 38 participants), aged healthy controls (≥65 years, n = 167) and AD (n = 19). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Each dot represents one participant. g, Embeddings of microglial trajectory-associated genes, colored by trajectory rank (left) or correlation with AD status (right).

a, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) for genes significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (18 AD samples from 6 donors, 21 control [CTL] samples from 7 donors). PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor (AD/control donors: astrocytes 313/165, microglia 312/165, oligodendrocytes 312/165, OPCs 313/165, endothelial cells 305/159). Both analyses used edgeR likelihood-ratio tests. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: astrocytes ρ = 0.656, n = 87 genes, P = 5.4 × 10−12. Microglia ρ = 0.588, n = 208, P = 9.7 × 10−21. Oligodendrocytes ρ = 0.894, n = 191, P = 1.2 × 10−67. OPCs ρ = 0.978, n = 17, P = 6.1 × 10−6. Endothelial cells ρ = −0.667, n = 8, P = 0.083. P values for OPCs and endothelial cells were computed exactly. The other three used the asymptotic t approximation because the exact algorithm underflowed. Dashed lines indicate zero. b, Age distribution of the 208 donors with microglia in the aging cohort. c, Homeostatic (blue), DAM1 (orange) and DAM2 (red) module scores versus age in the aging cohort (208 donors, 40,226 nuclei). Scores were averaged per donor and then per distinct age. Each point represents one of 64 age-level means. Lines show LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.6). Spearman ρ and two-sided, unadjusted P values were computed across the 64 age-level means. d, Expression of homeostatic (CSF1R, CX3CR1, P2RY12), DAM1 (APOE, B2M, CTSB) and DAM2 (AXL, CLEC7A, TIMP2) markers in the aging cohort. Left: per-nucleus expression versus donor age, with LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.5). Right: donors aged <65 years (149 donors, 31,118 nuclei) and ≥65 years (59 donors, 9,108 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Asterisks indicate Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR quasi-likelihood F-tests (≥65 versus <65 years, adjusted for sex, BH correction across all 34,176 genes): CX3CR1 3.0 × 10−3, P2RY12 1.7 × 10−2, APOE 3.3 × 10−8, B2M 1.8 × 10−4, AXL 1.1 × 10−2, CLEC7A 4.8 × 10−2. CSF1R (0.22), CTSB (0.26) and TIMP2 (0.51) were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and F statistics are in Supplementary Table 13. e, Age distribution of all 1,040 donors with microglia in the PsychAD AD cohort, including all diagnoses. Panels f and g use the 585 donors with a normal or AD diagnosis. f, Module scores as in c for the AD cohort (585 donors, 112,785 nuclei), computed across 59 age-level means. g, Expression as in d for the AD cohort: young controls (normal, <65 years, 95 donors, 18,764 nuclei), older controls (normal, ≥65 years, 165 donors, 28,330 nuclei), AD ≥ 65 years (312 donors, 63,760 nuclei) and early-onset AD (< 65 years, 13 donors, 1,931 nuclei). Asterisks indicate BH-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD ≥ 65 versus older controls, 1 d.f., BH correction across all genes): APOE 6.7 × 10−6, CX3CR1 5.5 × 10−3, TIMP2 1.7 × 10−2. Other markers were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and likelihood-ratio statistics are in Supplementary Table 13.

a, Dot plot displaying the expression of key marker genes enriched in distinct hypothalamic subregions, as inferred by marker from their expression. Dot size represents the fraction of nuclei within a neuronal subtype expressing the gene; color intensity indicates the mean normalized expression level. b, UMAP of the top 30 neuronal subclusters with the highest number of DEGs. c, Strip plot showing log2FC values for significant DEGs identified across all 254 neuronal subtypes. Points are colored to indicate the predominant inferred hypothalamic subregion of the neuronal subtype in which the DEG is found. d, Inferred spatial localization of top AD-altered neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

Inferred spatial localization of neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

a, Dot plots showing maximum and mean log-normalized expression of neuropeptide genes and receptors across all hypothalamic neurons (213,469 nuclei from all young, CTL, AD and AD_44 donors). Error bars in mean-expression plots show the standard deviation across nuclei. This panel is descriptive. b, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) in GABAergic (left) and glutamatergic (right) neurons. Each point represents a gene significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). For each gene and lineage, the result with the lowest FDR across constituent neuronal subtypes was selected. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (AD versus CTL, edgeR likelihood-ratio tests), whereas PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: GABAergic ρ = 0.028, n = 765 genes, P = 0.45. Glutamatergic ρ = 0.296, n = 301 genes, P = 1.7 × 10−7. Genes are correlation units, not biological replicates. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. Dashed lines indicate zero.

a, Ranked bar charts of univariate AUROC for distinguishing AD status using neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores (top) and MRI-derived volumetric measures (bottom). MRI participant counts are as in b. b, Cross-modal comparison of univariate AUROC between MRI-derived volume and neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores for matched hypothalamic regions (1:1 pairing). Left: snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC, with a dashed line indicating equal performance. Right: AUROC estimates for each modality by region, with lines connecting matched estimates. Each dot represents one AUROC estimate, not a biological replicate. No error bars or cross-modal tests are shown. Score direction was chosen so that AUROC ≥ 0.5. The dashed vertical line indicates chance (AUROC = 0.5). MRI AUROCs used 316 participants: 24 with AD, defined as cognitively impaired and amyloid-β positive, and 292 without AD. snRNA-seq AUROCs used donor-level pseudobulks from 14 biologically independent donors (7 AD, 7 control) for ARC, PVH, SCN, MN, PO, TM, ZI and the whole hypothalamus, 13 donors (7 AD, 6 control) for LH, and 10 donors (5 AD, 5 control) for VMH and DMH. c, Cross-modal comparison as in b, with snRNA-seq AUROC averaged across neuronal subregion annotations containing the matched region. For example, AN includes ARC, ARC_SCN, ARC_SMN, LH_ARC, PO_ARC, SCN_ARC, VMH_ARC and ZI_ARC. Left: mean snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC. Right: bars show MRI AUROC and mean snRNA-seq AUROC, and dots show individual annotation AUROCs. Error bars show sample standard deviations (n − 1 denominator) across annotations and appear only when at least three annotations match. Matching annotation counts are 8 (AN/ARC), 6 (Pa/PVH), 4 (VM/VMH), 10 (SCN), 2 (DM/DMH), 4 (MM/MN), 7 (MPO/PO), 1 (TM), 5 (ZI), 3 (LH) and 1 (whole hypothalamus). Standard deviations describe variation across annotations, not donor-level uncertainty. No inferential comparison was performed. All annotations originate from the same pool of 14 donors (7 AD, 7 control), so AUROCs averaged within a region are not statistically independent. MRI AUROCs and participant counts are as in b. AN and DM denote the arcuate nucleus and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (ARC and DMH in the main text).

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Fresh whole hypothalamus was obtained from eight 8-month-old female mice: four wild-type (WT) and four 5xFAD heterozygous (HET). Tissue underwent Dounce homogenization, debris cleanup and nuclei isolation. Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Chromium Controller, and 3′ gene-expression libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq platform, yielding 60,479 nuclei for analysis. b, UMAP of 60,479 nuclei, colored by major cell type: astrocytes, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, microglia, leukocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and fibroblasts. c, Cross-species cell-type correspondence. Heatmap of Spearman correlations between human HypoAD cell types (columns) and mouse 5xFAD cell types (rows), with mouse cell types labeled using transferred human annotations. #1319. Push it to the Max! Dowman, 16, becomes England U21s youngest-ever goalscorer - as Arsenal starlet scores 89th-minute winner against France

Published: 18:36 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:37 EST, 16 November 2026

Max Dowman broke another record as the 16-year-old became the youngest-ever goalscorer for England's Under-21 side on Monday night.

The Arsenal teenager has already broken a plethora of records at club level, and is now taking that to the international stage too, breaking a record set by senior team star Jude Bellingham, who scored aged 17 years and 67 days in 2020.

Dowman was called into the U21 squad for the first time this international break, and made his debut off the bench in the 1-0 defeat by Portugal on Friday.

On Monday, meanwhile, he was given a start by manager Lee Carsley, and rewarded his manager's faith with an 89th-minute winner to break the record and earn his side a 3-2 win.

It's a record he can add to his already-extensive collection, which includes being the youngest Champions League player, the youngest Premier League goalscorer, and the youngest Premier League winner.

Manager Lee Carsley said after the game: 'He played really well - he was one of four or five outstanding performances. Mikey Moore, Max, Ethan (Nwaneri), they were very good.

Max Dowman became England Under-21s' youngest-ever goal scorer when he scored against France on Monday

'We see how good on the ball he is but he was outstanding off the ball. You have to keep reminding yourself about his age. There's a lot of expectation around him and he seems to handle that so well.

'It's important we keep supporting him and he develops at his own pace. It's so important he enjoys his football.

'Obviously all the players in the squad are under pressure from their clubs and the expectation that surrounds them, so as much as we can we have to make that as easy as we can.'

Despite bursting onto the scene last season, Dowman has just 19 minutes to his name in the top flight this campaign as Arsenal look to defend their title.

He has played a number of games for the Gunners' U21 side, while he was sent off against League Two side Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup.

Arteta scolded his player at the time, but said: 'I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. Whether that's positive or negative. You need to understand the context, the relationship I have with him and what we discussed before we went out.

'If you see the reaction from my mother and father with me sometimes, you'd say "you don't like that reaction", but for me it was the best reaction ever as it enabled me to be who I am.

The Arsenal teenager, 16, broke the record held by Jude Bellingham with his late winner

'But you want to see the best and most beautiful reaction. You want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with 10 men.

'What do you expect? That's the level and that's the reaction. Whether it's right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, I'm f****d off, big time.

'This is the environment and the reality. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League. We look after him so much but we are also demanding as he needs to earn the right to play otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me?'

#1318. Cubarsí wins 2026 Golden Boy with 475 of 500 points as Barça reach five winners

Barcelona centre-back Pau Cubarsí, 19, has won Tuttosport's 2026 Golden Boy award for Europe's best under-21 player by a wide margin. The landslide puts a defender on top of a prize rarely won by one, and pushes Barcelona further clear as the club with the most winners.

This year’s vote was one-sided. No other candidate came close to the Barcelona defender.

The margin shows how settled the vote was. It also marks a rare win for a player in his position. Corriere dello Sport described him as only the second defender ever to win it. He succeeds PSG’s Désiré Doué, the 2025 winner.

Cubarsí now joins a club list that already featured Messi, Pedri, Gavi and Lamine Yamal. Four of the five have come in the last six years. Pedri won in 2021, Gavi in 2022 and Lamine Yamal in 2024.

No player can win the award twice. Each Barcelona success therefore means a different young player reaching the top of the vote. The recent run points to a steady flow of talent into the first team.

The award caps a strong year for the defender. He was a big part of Barcelona’s LaLiga and Super Cup wins. He was also named young player of the tournament as Spain won the World Cup. He started all eight of Spain’s games there. FIFA’s Young Player Award made him the first defender to receive it. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final. They kept seven clean sheets and conceded only once, in a 2-1 quarter-final win over Belgium. The Golden Boy arrives just weeks after he narrowly missed out on the Kopa Trophy.

Cubarsí was not the only Barcelona name on the list. Three of Monday’s winners came from the club. Joan Laporta took the Best President award. Barça Femení B’s Giulia Galli won the Best Italian Golden Girl prize. Outside the club, the Best Agent prize went to Jorge Mendes.

Laporta’s prize puts the club’s president alongside its young defender in the same announcement. Galli’s award extends the club’s haul to its women’s set-up. Together, the three prizes give Barcelona recognition across the boardroom, the men’s first team and the women’s game.

𝗣𝗔𝗨 𝗖𝗨𝗕𝗔𝗥𝗦𝗜, 𝗚𝗢𝗟𝗗𝗘𝗡 𝗕𝗢𝗬 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲✨ pic.twitter.com/y4LljnnhOg

The timing suits both club and country. Barcelona sit top of LaLiga. Spain have a decider against England coming up. For Cubarsí, the award adds individual recognition to a season already built on trophies.

The prizes will be handed out at a ceremony in Turin on 14 December. All three of Barcelona’s awards become official at that ceremony.

#1317. Blázquez double from Rioja assists seals Valencia’s 6-0 Copa del Rey win over Tavernes

Aimar Blázquez scored twice from Rioja assists as Valencia beat Tavernes 6-0 at Mestalla, where the hosts were officially the away side. The win follows a 0-3 defeat to Real Madrid and takes Valencia into the second round.

Valencia cruised past Tavernes in the Copa del Rey on Tuesday 10 November 2026. The tie was played at the Estadio de Mestalla, yet Valencia were officially the away side in their own stadium. The RFEF had granted Tavernes’ request to stage the match there.

Raba opened the scoring in the first minute, with Blázquez providing the assist. Raba then turned provider for Duro in the 11th minute. Rioja added the third in the 19th minute after a pass from Martinez. A fourth goal arrived through Elliott in the 23rd minute.

Tavernes goalkeeper Mainar kept the margin there three minutes into the second half. He saved a header from Blázquez, who had been set up by Raba. The number 37 struck in the 57th minute and again in the 69th. Danjuma replaced him after 70 minutes, when Gayà also came on for Rioja.

Three players were booked. Ugrinic was cautioned in the ninth minute and Montilla of Tavernes in the 22nd. Rioja picked up a yellow card in the 49th minute.

Tavernes came closest to a goal when Erik struck the post after a short corner. EFE described the visitors as a sixth-tier club and reported that close to 40 coaches carried their fans to Mestalla. Their municipal ground was not fit for the tie. Mestalla is in its final season before the move to Nou Mestalla.

A 9pm start had been planned for the tie. Every Copa del Rey match scheduled for that day was called off by the RFEF, and this one was among them.

Tavernes reached the first round through the two-legged preliminary round against UD Maracena. The first leg was played at the CD Maracena ground on Sunday 27 September 2026. The two sides drew 1-1 and 0-0.

For Valencia, the Real Madrid loss had itself followed a 1-0 win over Elche and a 1-2 defeat to Villarreal. Javier Aguirre said he took positive conclusions from the tie. He welcomed the return of players who had been out long-term. He also said Valencia now need to win in the league.

Aimar Blazquez scored a brace for Valencia as they pummeled Tavernes to advance to the next round of the Spanish Copa Del Rey pic.twitter.com/sgzCjeOecT

— Football with Osadolor (@osa_dolor) November 11, 2026

The cup calendar continues with the round of 32 on 16 December. The last 16 follows on 6 January and the quarter-finals on 13 January. The semi-finals are the only two-legged round, with first legs on 10 February and second legs on 3 March. The competition runs until 24 April 2027.

Valencia return to league action away to Rayo Vallecano at the Estadio de Vallecas on Saturday 21 November.

#1316. Florian Wirtz scores twice (including a stunner) as Germany thump Netherlands 5-0 in UEFA Nations League... as Liverpool misfit receives a hug from Jurgen Klopp after impressing

Published: 17:56 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 19:19 EST, 16 November 2026

Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.

The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.

And he continued that trend on Monday evening with two goals for his side to help them top their Nations League group.

His first was the pick of the bunch. Wirtz moved along the forward line as a Dutch side without Virgil van Dijk struggled to contain him. He picked up the ball around 25 yards out, cut inside onto his weaker left foot, and curled a pearling effort into the far corner off the post.

That goal, which came on the hour mark, put his side 2-0 up after Freiburg's Derry Scherhant had scored the opener, and Wirtz wasn't done there.

Centre back Nico Schlotterbeck made it 3-0 before the Liverpool man picked up his second of the night after drifting into the penalty box unmarked and finishing high after good work from Brajan Gruda.

Cette version de Wirtz avec le maillot de la Mannschaft c’est celle qu’on aimerait voir chaque semaine en PL. Quel missile pour faire le break ! Meilleur buteur allemand sur cette édition de l’UNL. 🇩🇪🔥 pic.twitter.com/m0DqaOungS

Florian Wirtz scored a brace for Germany as they thumped the Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League action

Liverpool midfielder Wirtz received a big hug from a smiling Jurgen Klopp at full time

Gruda himself, who is on loan at RB Leipzig from Brighton, wrapped up the five-star win on a night that arguably saw Klopp announce himself as Germany boss.

After full-time, the ex-Liverpool manager gave Wirtz a huge hug as the duo beamed with big smiles on their faces.

While it was a night to remember for Germany, a Netherlands team that included the likes of Micky van de Ven, Jurrien Timber and Wirtz's Liverpool team-mate Cody Gakpo were left exasperated.

Van Dijk had pulled out of the squad with a knock after playing with a knock in recent weeks.

His side will still, though, compete in the Nations League quarter-finals after finishing second in the group, finishing ahead of Greece on goal difference.

As for Wirtz, he will hope his performance will help continue what has been an uphill climb so far this season.

He also found the net for Germany in their first match of the international break – a 3-1 win over Serbia – and picked up a goal and assist in Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace before the international break.

In total, he has two goals and five assists in 15 games for Liverpool this season – though the Reds will hope those numbers increase as the season goes on.

His second goal came as he drifted into the penalty area and finished high into the net

Last month, meanwhile, Reds manager Andoni Iraola insisted he has full faith in his midfielder.

'I think he has had a little bit of everything this season,' he said. 'He has had good games, probably the other day was not his best game, especially offensively. We trust Florian.

'Florian is a very good player. He was coming from good performances in the international break, I think. I think it is a matter of everyone to find his moment.'

Klopp hailed him 'exceptional', meanwhile, during the last international break.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

However, Pochettino had a $10 million release clause in his contract and spoke multiple times about his desire to go back to the English Premier League, after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea before making his move to the U.S.

Manchester United have also explored multiple options in the past weeks, and several names emerged as potential candidates for the job. Let's take a look at the top free-agent coaches currently available on the market and identify those who remain open to a move in the near future. For this specific reason we have decided to not include former Manchester City coach Pep Guardiola, who is not looking for a job in the short term.

The Spanish coach left Manchester City ahead of the summer of 2026 and decided to take a break from the world of soccer, despite having a concrete offer in the summer to become the new manager of the Italian national team. Guardiola sat down with the Italian federation but then opted to stick to his commitment to take a break. Furthermore, given his close ties to the Manchester City hierarchy and ownership, his name was never going to be considered by the Manchester United board. Here's a list of the top coaches without a job right now:

The former England national team manager is still searching for his next club after deciding to step down from his international role in order to return to club management. However, he appears unlikely to find a new position in the short term. This is a challenge currently facing several national team coaches, including former France manager Didier Deschamps. Manchester United had previously shown interest in him, but did not make a concrete approach in recent weeks, despite having the opportunity to do so.

The former Tottenham manager was one of the names that emerged in the past weeks for the Man United job. The former Newcastle head coach was one of the names on the list of the Manchester United board of directors in recent weeks. The English head coach left Newcastle in the summer and he's still under contract with the club right now. Any club looking to appoint him would first have to pay a release clause to Newcastle. Despite his Premier League experience, Manchester United did not consider him as a potential replacement. He is now likely to wait until the summer before deciding on his next career move.

An attractive name: the former German national team coach left his job in the summer after the disappointment of the 2026 World Cup, when Germany were kicked out by Paraguay in the round of 32 of the tournament. Nagelsmann, after coaching RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich before moving to the national team, is now likely to move to another league, and the Premier League is definitely a league that can potentially attract him. Let's now see if there will be a job available in the summer, even if the big clubs seem pretty stable at this stage.

The Italian coach is waiting for the right opportunity to come after the two years spent at Napoli, where he was able to win the Scudetto in his first season in charge, replicating the success he had at Juventus and Inter in his home country. According to reports, Conte would be keen for another Premier League experience after coaching Chelsea and Tottenham but he's not ruling out other clubs. However, Manchester United never made contact with his camp as they didn't want to hire the Italian manager to replace Carrick. Real Madrid are holding off on any verdict over Aurélien Tchouaméni. The midfielder has returned from international duty with a familiar problem in his right adductor. Yet he has not been ruled out of the Celta game at the Santiago Bernabéu.

The French Football Federation said in an official statement on 10 November that it had sent him back to Madrid after talking to Real Madrid’s doctors. France’s medical staff took his medical history into account. The decision was made with the player’s agreement. He was due to spend the night with the squad and fly to Madrid the next day. France will not replace him.

The problem had troubled him since he reported to Clairefontaine. Tchouaméni had been unable to finish France’s training session on Tuesday. He became the third player to leave the squad during this get-together, after Pierre Kalulu and Marcus Thuram.

The picture in Madrid is less clear-cut than France’s decision might suggest. First checks found discomfort in his right groin area, according to Cadena COPE. Radiological and physical tests were set to begin on Thursday.

Tchouaméni is a key starter for Mourinho. He started the 3-0 win at Valencia before the break. That result was Madrid’s eighth win in a row across LaLiga and the Champions League. Mbappé scored for the seventh match running.

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. #1312. Inside Gotham FC's move to Icahn Stadium: Debates over pitch quality, fines and the NWSL's logistical struggle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Juan Carlos Amoros is always subtle in demeanor, down to his usual all-black attire, so after Gotham FC's uninspiring 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign on Sunday, his subdued tone was hardly a surprise. His post-match remarks, though, were a departure from the victory lap a coach might take after winning in the NWSL quarterfinals.

"I feel the obligation to almost apologize for the state of the pitch," Amoros said. "I think at this level, in this kind of game, as a league, we should be having a better surface. Unfortunately, our football club did absolutely everything in their power to make sure that was the case. Unfortunately, it wasn't but luckily, it looks like nobody got hurt and the game was what it was."

He was hardly the only one to mention the grass at Sports Illustrated Stadium. It seeped its way into every post-match media availability, dominated conversation between the players and was a talking point amongst staff working that day. A dull stretch of grass with yellow-green splotches overshadowed one of the most important matches of the NWSL's season – and put the league on course for an unlikely downsize for Sunday's playoff semifinal between Gotham and the Kansas City Current.

Roughly 24 hours after Amoros' apology, Gotham moved Sunday's game to Icahn Stadium, a 5,000-seater on Manhattan's Randall's Island that they have played at just twice before. Sports Illustrated Stadium, the 25,000-seat venue in Harrison, N.J. that Gotham have called home since 2021, was available but concerns about player safety prompted an unwanted last-minute move.

"We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth," Gotham captain Tierna Davidson said in a statement on Monday. "What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league or our fans deserve. The quality of the game is not up for debate, so we've made the difficult decision to move to Icahn Stadium on Sunday. A smaller stadium means many of you will not be there, and that is the hardest part of this decision."

Monday's announcement was the final stage of a back-and-forth between Gotham and MLS' Red Bull New York, the primary tenants and operators of Sports Illustrated Stadium, one that highlights the logistical nightmares that have unexpectedly disrupted the NWSL's postseason.

MLS' World Cup break this summer afforded RBNY the chance to install a new pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium, the process complete by the team's July 25 loss to Charlotte FC. It was the perfect time for a reset ahead of a busy schedule for the new field – 17 other matches were a guarantee, while the potential postseason runs for both RBNY and Gotham meant the number could stretch well over 20 games before the year was over.

By the time Gotham had secured a home quarterfinal with a draw against Angel City on Oct. 4, there was little reason to suspect that the playing surface would become an issue. Matches are rarely relocated because of pitch quality concerns and the field at Sports Illustrated Stadium has historically been one of American soccer's best; it won the Sports Turf Management Association's award for professional soccer fields in 2021, the year Gotham moved in. The NWSL team did not have another home game until Nov. 1, a period in which RBNY played three home games and the stadium hosted a USA Rugby Fall Series doubleheader. Sometime before the early November fixture against the Royals, Gotham raised concerns with their landlords about the field conditions, the scars of the rugby games on Oct. 30 notably visible.

Nothing came of those complaints, though, and so the Royals match went on as scheduled but the conditions did not go unnoticed. The NWSL imposed a $10,000 fine on Gotham for the state of the field, even though they do not manage the venue as secondary tenants. The fine was not widely known – the NWSL Players Association said it was unaware of the punishment, while a source with knowledge of the matter said RBNY also did not know. Many found out about the fine after Reign head coach Laura Harvey mentioned it in a post-match press conference after the quarterfinal, but worry about the quality of the grass had already reached a fever pitch at that point.

Despite the fine, a field consultant working on the NWSL's behalf inspected the pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium on Friday and declared that it met FIFA standards. The following day, RBNY hosted their regular season finale against Atlanta United and less than 18 hours later, another group took a look at the field in the hours building up to Gotham's win over the Reign. It was deemed playable on Sunday morning by representatives from the NWSL, the Professional Referee Organization and the NWSLPA, according to a source familiar with the situation.

Even from a distance, the grass appeared problematic. The sand that was left over from the rugby doubleheader still lined the pitch, while some rugby lines were faint but visible in certain spots. The players' review of the surface, though, was damning – Harvey called it "s---," Reign captain Jess Fishlock said it was "atrocious," and Gotham midfielder Jaelin Howell described it as "sandy" and "unstable." Gotham attacker Jaedyn Shaw also expressed concern that her planted foot would slip during corner kicks and all agreed that it ultimately impacted the teams' ability to compete.

lower bowl isn’t quite full at kickoff between Gotham and the Seattle Reign, though there are some fans in the upper bowlGotham announced earlier that they sold 3,000 tickets through NYC Mayor Mamdani’s offer (including 1,000 in the first 10 minutes of sale)#NWSL pic.twitter.com/qviBM65bsz

Gotham, in conjunction with the NWSL, spent the hours after their quarterfinal win discussing options with RBNY to improve the playing surface. The main solutions, according to multiple sources, were re-sodding the pitch – essentially ripping the existing field out and installing a new one – or a hybrid model in which artificial threads would be stitched into the existing grass. Both would be timely endeavors – the former would be longer while the latter might have been completed in time for Gotham to host the Current on Sunday.

There was just one problem. RBNY have a friendly against Club America scheduled for Saturday.

The game will serve as the final match of their season after they missed the MLS Cup playoffs and takes place during the men's international break, which means some players from both teams will be tied up with their national teams instead. Multiple sources said the NWSL could not guarantee that the hybrid model project would not actually be completed in time for RBNY's friendly on Saturday evening, even if it would have been ready in time for Gotham's Sunday afternoon game against the Current. RBNY were unwilling to proceed with the hybrid plan, as a result, and so Gotham chose to leave Sports Illustrated Stadium for Icahn Stadium.

RBNY still intend to play on the pitch that NWSL players complained about on Saturday and no changes to the field are expected to be made beforehand.

"We understand how frustrating the move is for Gotham and their fans. We had hoped to see Gotham continue its championship run at Sports Illustrated Stadium, too," RBNY said in a statement. "We invest in the pitch year-round, with a dedicated grounds team and specialist field partners, and it was cleared for every match played there this season. Those inspections continue for all remaining events this year. We worked closely with Gotham and the NWSL to address their concerns, but unfortunately the experts and the league couldn't guarantee the additional work they wanted to be completed could be done in time. We wish Gotham the best in their match."

The venue is not brand new to Gotham, who have hosted two games at the stadium in the last two years, and seems well-equipped to at least solve the main problem they faced at Sports Illustrated Stadium. Amoros complimented the quality of Icahn Stadium's pitch when Gotham hosted a Concacaf W Champions Cup group stage game there in Aug. 2025. Though it did not prompt Gotham's selection of Icahn Stadium to host that match, the New Jersey venue's field had also looked suboptimal in the run-up to the continental clash. RBNY subsequently replaced the pitch during that period, weeks before the U.S. men's national team played a friendly against South Korea on Sept. 6 last year.

"I don't really want to talk too much about it but the Sports Illustrated Stadium has traditionally been the best pitch in the league," Amoros said at the time, "and the last couple of games, it's definitely been far away from that so this pitch here is outstanding."

Gotham's last-minute switch to Icahn Stadium was a surprise in large part because an entirely separate scheduling issue had overshadowed the first week of the postseason.

The NWSL had two broadcast slots for the semifinals, Saturday at noon ET on CBS and Sunday at 3 p.m. ET on ABC, but did not exactly have the first-choice venues to host them. RBNY's Saturday friendly locked Gotham out of that time slot entirely if they wanted to play at Sports Illustrated Stadium, but they needed the Washington Spirit to beat the Portland Thorns for the Sunday window since the Thorns would be unable to hold a game that kicked off at 9 a.m. local time. The Spirit's lopsided win guaranteed Gotham would play on Sunday but they had their own issues – the Secretaries' Cup, a Division III college football game between the United States Merchant Marine Academy and the United States Coast Guard Academy, was taking place at Audi Field during the Saturday time slot.

The Spirit seemed destined for a semifinal at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., home of the NFL's Washington Commanders and a stadium they had never played in before, but late discussions with Audi Field's owners, MLS' D.C. United, and a contribution from sponsor Lafayette Federal Credit Union to underwrite the costs of the schedule change meant that problem was solved.

Gotham's move to Icahn Stadium, though, only reinforced the logistical issues that the NWSL has battled for its entire existence. The optics have favored the league in recent years, with the vast majority of their teams playing in state-of-the-art soccer-specific stadiums and managing to survive the constant game of venue Tetris. Scheduling conflicts, though, were never out of the realm of possibility, and many have marred the league this year. The Boston Legacy, for example, had to move home games from Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass. to Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, R.I., during the World Cup and will play there in 2027 while the construction project continues on Boston's White Stadium.

The issues that plagued Gotham and the Spirit, though, are in line with a different problem – control over facilities. Around half of the league's teams are secondary tenants in the stadiums they play in, so management of the venues is almost entirely out of their hands. It is unclear how quickly that will change for any of those teams. Gotham will leave Sports Illustrated Stadium for Etihad Park in 2028, but that stadium will be managed by MLS' New York City FC. They will continue to be secondary tenants in that building, which technically means they could be subject to the same problems they currently face. MLS' calendar flip next year will likely see the issue morph but not necessarily change. The leagues' postseason schedules will be different for the foreseeable future but teams like Gotham and the Spirit will still be at the mercy of their landlords in the meantime; Gotham's conflict with RBNY an example of just that. RBNY's friendly was the sticking point in their discussions over the pitch and ultimately took precedence over an NWSL semifinal.

Control over venues continues to weigh heavily in the NWSL's expansion process and is a key part of the issue that causes the most hand-wringing in the league's front office – the calendar. The Current might be the NWSL's gold standard as the owners and operators of CPKC Stadium, though they have been hamstrung by the NWSL's scheduling issues. Kickoff of their quarterfinal win over Angel City was at 11:30 a.m. local time because they were the only team able to take that broadcast slot on CBS. The since-ousted San Diego Wave could not host a game with a 9:30 a.m. local kickoff, while Gotham and the Spirit were locked out of their venues because of MLS matches on the same day.

There is a meet-in-the-middle approach, one that the NWSL might use as often as they can as the expansion process continues. A handful of teams share ownership groups with MLS teams, who chiefly own and operate their own stadiums and tend to treat the NWSL teams as equal tenants. The number will grow in 2028 when teams in Atlanta and Columbus, both owned by the local MLS clubs, will join the league.

#1311. Tony Mowbray steps down as Blackburn Rovers manager with immediate effect due to health reasons - two years after bowel cancer battle forced him to leave Birmingham City

Published: 05:25 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 08:02 EST, 17 November 2026

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers manager due to ill health.

The 62-year-old, who previously had to walk away from his job at Birmingham City in 2024 due to a battle with bowel cancer, leaves Blackburn with immediate effect.

The Championship side announced his departure with a statement from Mowbray. It read: 'Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as Head Coach of Blackburn Rovers.

'I’m immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I’ve loved working with them.

'Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you’ve given me. It’s been a pleasure working alongside you.

'To the fans, thank you for the way you’ve supported me and the team this season. I’ve always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers boss due to ill health

'I’m grateful to the Owners and Suhail (Pasha, chief operating officer) for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

Mowbray leaves with Blackburn 13th in the Championship. He took over at the club in June this year having spent two years out of the game following his health issues at Birmingham City.

The veteran manager suddenly stepped down as manager of Birmingham in February 2024 after undergoing surgery for bowel cancer. He had 15cm of his bowel removed during his treatment.

He took a temporary leave of absence after eight games in charge, before officially resigning from the role in May.

Mowbray, who has managed a host of English clubs, opened up publicly about his struggles, telling the Times that his children had feared the worst.

'I had the conversation with my family and you could see they were frightened,' he said. 'Was I frightened? My only thoughts were for my family, my three children and my wife and making sure they were OK.

'I had to put everything in order and I tried to. My wife saw our banking app for the first time in her life. It's little things like that. She understood. This was serious stuff. I felt she needed to know where we had our money, whether it was ISAs or pensions and what was in the bank.'

Speaking on his diagnosis, which came after he collapsed when trying to answer the door, he added: 'My wife put me in the car and drove me back to hospital and they wanted to know why I was collapsing and in the condition I was,' he says. 'They rehydrated me and put me on a drip overnight.

'I remember sitting there in bed and my kids' eyes were watering up. They were scared I wasn't going to live. How old were they? They were 15, 17 and 19. I could see the fear in their eyes.'

Mowbray's comeback story when he was made Blackburn boss in the summer was one of the feel-good moments of the offseason. It has not been disclosed what his current health issue is.

Mowbray leaves Blackburn with the team in 13th place in the Championship table

Blackburn Rovers owner Balaji Rao added his own statement, writing: 'Our thoughts are with Tony and his family as he steps back from his duties to focus on his health.

'Through our many meetings over the years, we’ve come to know Tony well and grown very fond of him. We’ve always admired his professionalism, his dedication and the passion he brings to his work at Blackburn Rovers.

'Tony, please know that you have our unconditional and unwavering support. We send you and your family our love and strength, and we will do all we can to support you through this time.'

Chief Executive Officer Steve Curwood said: 'Tony’s passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much.

'Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can.

'On behalf of everyone at Blackburn Rovers, I would like to send Tony and his family our very best wishes during this time.'

#1310. Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers1,2,3,4,8,9. Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8+ T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies10,11,12,13. However, ferroptotic cells limit this response8,9,10,14, resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE2 production or disrupting PGE2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15. Cancer cells are commonly protected from unrestrained lipid peroxidation and spontaneous ferroptotic cell death by molecular defence systems such as the system xc––glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) pathway5,16, in which GPX4 is the key enzyme mediating lipid peroxide detoxification. Strategies to promote ferroptosis by blockade of ferroptosis defence systems, such as GPX4 inhibitors, have been considered promising approaches to achieve tumour elimination in patients with difficult-to-treat cancers8,9. Studies using preclinical mouse models have uncovered that effective tumour elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies requires anticancer immunity by DCs10 and tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells11,12,13. Yet recent findings have suggested that DC-driven anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity is suppressed in ferroptotic tumours8,9,10,17. Emerging evidence has implicated that the unrestrained generation of membrane lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells can promote the production and release of molecules that may impact immune cell functions18. However, what causes the suppression of DC-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity in the context of tumour ferroptosis remains largely unclear.

Potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15. To assess ferroptosis-induced oxylipin production and identify key factors, we profiled the oxylipin secretome of mouse BRAF(V600E) and NRAS(G12D) melanoma, 4T1 breast cancer and MC38 colorectal cancer cells following RSL3-induced ferroptosis. Across all these cancer cell lines, RSL3-treated (ferroptotic) cells displayed increased production of oxylipins compared with untreated (non-ferroptotic) controls (Fig. 1a). Of note, in all groups, the eicosanoid PGE2 was by far the most abundant oxylipin upregulated by ferroptosis induction (Fig. 1a). Similar to ferroptosis induction by RSL3 (which inhibits selenoproteins beyond GPX4), we observed strong PGE2 production after genetic ablation of the ferroptosis-protective enzyme GPX4, ferroptosis induction using the GPX4 inhibitor ML210 or erastin-mediated inactivation of system xc–-mediated cystine import (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). Thus, ferroptosis may trigger the production of PGE2 in cancer cells, which is a notable finding given the important role of PGE2 for suppression of anticancer immunity19,20,21.

NS, not significant. c–f, Functional analyses of cDC1s exposed to dying cancer cell conditioned medium (CM). Experimental design (c). CXCL9 production by cDC1s; the plots show one cDC1 culture representative of n = 4 cultures (d). Quantification of CXCL9+ cDC1s, based on panel d; n = 4 samples (e). Analysis of cDC1s by RNA-seq (n = 4); the volcano plots show the effect of CM from ferroptotic (left) or apoptotic (right) BRAF(V600E) cells on activation-induced cDC1 genes (f). PE, phycoerythrin; RNA-seq, RNA sequencing; SSC-A, side scatter area. Data show mean ± s.e.m. of n = 3 biological replicates (a). In b, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. In e, the centre line indicates the median, the bounds extend from the 25th to the 75th percentile, and the whiskers correspond to he minimum and maximum values. P values are from one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (two-sided; b,e). Differentially expressed genes were identified using a two-sided Wald test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (f).

By contrast, stimulation of ultraviolet B (UVB)-induced apoptosis, doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death or necrocide 1 (NC1)-induced necrotic cell death failed to promote PGE2 production (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1g). However, PGE2 production was induced in cells undergoing necroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 1h). These findings imply that PGE2 production is selectively induced by as yet unknown molecular events in ferroptotic cells and that these events, at least to some extent, may be shared with necroptotic cells.

Using liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), we further validated that ferroptotic cancer cells depend on lipid peroxides to produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This was not the case for key effectors of other cell death pathways, such as caspases or receptor-interacting serine–threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1; Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We extended our analyses to a broader panel of mouse and human cancer cells, including established cell lines, cells from spontaneous mouse cancer models and cells from patients with pancreatic cancer. In all these cells, RSL3-induced ferroptosis triggered markedly increased PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Together, these data suggest that ferroptosis promotes aberrant production of PGE2 in mouse and human cancer cells, prompting us to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms and consequences for anticancer immunity.

Effective anticancer immunity often depends on cDC1s22,23, which fulfil essential roles in the priming of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses24,25 and effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating T lymphocytes (TILs)26,27. These cDC1 functions are impacted by immunoregulatory factors derived from dying cancer cells22,23,28; however, how mediators released by ferroptotic cancer cells impact cDC1s and their functions is not known.

To address this issue, we generated cDC1s from bone marrow cells, exposed them to conditioned medium from RSL3-induced, ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells and assessed their functional properties after activation with polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly(I:C); Fig. 1c). The conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells strongly compromised the capacity of cDC1s to produce CXCL9 (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a), a chemokine required for cDC1-mediated orchestration of CD8+ TIL responses26,29. Similar results were observed for cDC1 production of the T cell stimulatory cytokine interleukin-12 (IL-12)30 (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). By contrast, no impairment was observed for cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from cancer cells undergoing apoptosis or doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Impaired CXCL9 production was similarly observed for splenic cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 3d). These results suggest that factors released by ferroptotic cancer cells disable cDC1s from producing molecules required to promote anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity.

cDC1 functions are controlled by transcriptional programming31,32. We therefore subjected cDC1s activated by poly(I:C) following exposure to ferroptotic or apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cell conditioned medium to transcriptional profiling by RNA sequencing. We found that ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, cancer cell-derived factors induced prominent transcriptional changes in cDC1s (Fig. 1f), including impaired expression of genes encoding stimulatory cytokines (including Ifnb and Ifnl2), T cell-recruiting chemokines (Cxcl9 and Ccl4) and integrins important for T cell activation (Itgal; Fig. 1f). We also confirmed the inhibitory effect on cDC1 cytokine and chemokine production at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Of note, we did not detect a defect in upregulation of MHC or costimulatory molecules (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1), implying that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors do not prevent cDC1 activation. Of note, many of the genes impaired in cDC1s following exposure to ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors were shared with a core gene set of PGE2-mediated cDC1 dysfunction (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 1), although genes beyond this set were also impaired. Consistently, gene set enrichment analyses revealed a prominent impairment of PGE2-regulated functional cDC1 genes (Extended Data Fig. 3h), whereas genes associated with migration or antigen processing (that is, molecular programs not regulated by PGE2 signalling in cDC1s19), remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 3h). Together, these data suggest that ferroptotic cancer cells promote cDC1 dysfunction and that this is mediated by PGE2.

Similar to cancer cells, ferroptosis induction caused aberrant PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a), an established mouse embryonic fibroblast model often used to study the molecular underpinnings of ferroptosis33. This was linked to markedly increased transcript and protein expression of the key PGE2-producing enzyme COX2 (encoded by Ptgs2; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Lip-1 treatment rescued this effect (Fig. 2a), whereas stimulation of lipid peroxidation by cumene hydroperoxide promoted both Ptgs2 expression and increased PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Together, these results point towards a requirement of membrane lipid peroxide generation for PGE2 production through transcriptional regulation of COX2. Using COX inhibitors, we also confirmed that COX activity was required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2b), but dispensable for execution of ferroptotic cell death (Fig. 2c).

Effect of CXB (1, 10 or 100 nM) or acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) (1, 10 or 100 µM) on PGE2 production (b) and cell viability (c); n = 3 samples. Effect of PEG treatment; n = 3 samples (g–j): experimental design (g); quantification of Ptgs2 mRNA (h) and COX2 protein (i) expression after 8 h; and measurement of PGE2 production (j).
