Fans could get a glimpse of a future round when Arsenal take on OL Lyonnes on Thursday. The Gunners now have the tall task of tackling the French giants after battling Barcelona to a 1-1 draw at Camp Nou last week.

A strong team defensive performance, anchored by goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez against the current title holders, and the inclusion of Frida Maanum in the attack were key difference-makers. Manager Renee Slegers and her side seem to be turning the page, with better results after questionable tactics and player availability raised concerns about the club's earlier performances.

Taking on OL Lyonnes also won't be easy. The top French side has scored 20 goals through four league phase matches, and Marie-Antoinette Katoto leads the competition's Golden Boot race with seven goals. U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes is getting more lethal in the tournament and scored in her second consecutive tournament match during OL's 6-0 blowout against Juventus.

Lily Yohannes makes it FOUR 💥The USWNT midfielder has now scored in back-to-back UWCL matches 🇺🇸🔥Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/9uLM309RM4

The eight-time Champions League winners will go up against an English club with plenty of momentum following last week's results against Barcelona. The Gunners have more players available to shake things up on the pitch, and Alessia Russo remains a threat after her hat trick against Benfica and has four goals in the league phase.

Chelsea FC will host PSG and the Blues are riding high on stout defensive performances. They co-lead the tournament alongside OL Lyonnes with zero goals conceded through four league phase games.

The London side will need to be far better in attack if they want to claim being a top contender, though it's not for lack of trying. They're coming off a scoreless draw against BK Hacken, where they recorded a whopping 32 shots but only six attempts on target. U.S. women's national team winger Alyssa Thompson is still a factor with her swift technique and could help stretch PSG's backline, while Wieke Kaptein gets into dangerous spaces. Kaptein created both goals in Chelsea's 2-0 win against Roma, and the Dutch player has one goal and two assists in the tournament.

PSG's fortunes seem to be turning for the worse after a promising start to the competition. They're in 10th place on the table now with five points and just one win in their last four games. The loss of Sakina Karchaoui with an ankle injury for the remainder of the league phase is a blow to the roster, though Naomie Feller, with two goals and two assists, is a threat for the Parisians.

There are plenty of teams on the lower side of the table and running out of time. Alongside PSG with necessary urgency are Juventus, who were just beaten by OL Lyonnes, 6-0, and face a desperate 17th-place OH Leuven before closing out the league phase against PSG. It makes the penultimate meeting with OH Leuven almost a must win for Juventus, to lessen the stress on the final matchday.

A particularly intriguing matchup between ninth-place Benfica and 12th-place Roma could shake up the league table with a win by either side. If Roma's Kayleigh van Dooren and Alayah Pilgrim stay active on offense again, it could be a tough challenge for Benfica.

In a farewell for Mauricio Pochettino before he heads to Manchester United, the United States men's national team were able to defeat Haiti 2-0 on Tuesday night, advancing in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals 8-0 on aggregate. Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with a bicycle-kick goal to kick things off, which was the emphatic send-off that was needed prior to Pochettino arriving in Manchester, but the USMNT were able to keep things up in the celebration in Cincinnati.

CHRISTIAN PULISIC GET ON YOUR BIKE‼️#USMNT x @VW pic.twitter.com/Yb3yqXfC33

Julian Hall followed with a poacher's goal as Weston McKennie played orchestrator, and it continued a theme that whoever ends up taking over the national team will have tough decisions ahead. Folarin Balogun is struggling for minutes with Monaco and is looking to make a move at the end of the season, and Hall has done everything that he can to increase his own standing with five goals in six games for the USMNT.

The New York Red Bulls star has a ways to go considering that he's still only 18 and will need to gain experience against top teams in the world instead of just Haiti, but he also can't ask for a better start than what he has gotten off to. It's why this is such an attractive job for whoever takes over the USMNT. They'll be able to build upon the good that Pochettino has instilled; the talent is there to move the squad forward, and there's plenty to love about the youth of the USMNT.

And alongside that, Pulisic has essentially screamed don't forget about me. During this camp, the Milan man has followed up on signing a new contract with the club by reaching 35 national team goals, moving into fourth all time for the USMNT over Eric Wynalda. Diego Kochen added to the good vibes with a third straight clean sheet, and Neil Pierre was even able to be cap-tied against the nation that he's also eligible for as the full-circle moments were left and right.

Pulisic, the former 17-year-old phenom, was subbed off for Cavan Sullivan, the current 17-year-old phenom, and while the goal difference may have been larger in the first leg between these sides, this felt like a more measured performance despite the strangeness of Pochettino's assistants heading to United while he managed the squad prior to catching his own charter.

This camp had every chance of being a disaster given the circumstances of Pochettino leaving, but all parties did what was needed during this camp. All dual nationals were capped, including Santiago Castaneda, showing that even on his way out, Pochettino made sure to take care of the future of the federation. On to the next round of the Concacaf Nations League with a new manager and no complaints with the performance so far for the squad.

#1274. Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network—a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers1,2,3 and 2D bilayers4, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO3 (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns. Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM) reveals a beam deflection texture in registry with the interfacial dislocation network. A machine learning interatomic potential, trained on first-principles calculations, together with phase-field modelling, confirms that competing strains within the dislocation network stabilize polar vortex–antivortex pairs; first-principles calculations further reveal the emergence of an electronic superlattice with a well-defined periodicity. Our results establish twist-controlled dislocation networks as a new and versatile route to designing local polar and electronic structures in oxide materials.

#1272. JJ Gabriel catches Man United by surprise after confirming exit: Star, 16, posts farewell video as he finalises move to Real Madrid after stunning Old Trafford chiefs with quit bombshell

Published: 13:58 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 15:07 EST, 17 November 2026

Sixteen-year-old JJ Gabriel has announced his departure from Manchester United, two months on from stunning club officials with his desire to leave.

Gabriel and his representatives made a bombshell request to have his academy contract torn up in September. That request was immediately refused by United and, while there was faint hope that a compromise could have been found to keep him at Old Trafford, he has stayed away ever since.

He has been training in Madrid in recent days ahead of a move to Real Madrid, and has taken to social media to bid farewell to the Red Devils after six years at the club.

Gabriel’s announcement is thought to have caught United by surprise, with the club first learning about it when the video appeared on social media. It’s understood that United haven’t heard from the player’s family since he was last seen at Carrington in September.

Despite his clear intention to sign for Madrid, United’s stance hasn’t changed and they still believe it will require FIFA’s approval for any move to go through.

'Dear Manchester United,' he began. 'I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams.

JJ Gabriel has confirmed his Manchester United exit online ahead of a move to Real Madrid

The 16-year-old penned a speech to the club, which he read out in a post (Instagram/jjnr10)

'Here I grew as a player and as a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award. You gave me moments I’ll always treasure.

'To every coach, member of staff, team-mate, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow. As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything. JJ.'

Daily Mail Sport exclusively revealed Madrid's growing confidence in securing the free-scoring starlet back in September. Gabriel has now secured a European Union passport through his mother's Cypriot heritage, and sources familiar with the situation believe a switch is imminent.

It is understood Gabriel will play for Madrid's Castilla team, which plays in Spain's third division, as well as in the Youth League.

Gabriel broke a series of records playing for United youth teams, including becoming the youngest player to feature in the Under-18s. Gabriel was 14 and scored twice on his debut.

He has also played – and scored – for the Under-21 side.

Gabriel, who turned 16 last month, is one of the brightest young talents in the world and his exit represents a huge loss to United.

As Daily Mail Sport previously reported, United's decline since the days of Sir Alex Ferguson has been the driving force behind Gabriel's family seeking an exit. United have not won a Premier League title since 2013.

United's decline since the days of Sir Alex Ferguson led to Gabriel's family seeking an exit

A source close to the family explained that United are 'far away' from the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, as well as domestic rivals Arsenal and Manchester City, and that they want him to 'learn from the best' to maximise his talents.

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill. His father, Joe O'Cearuill, changed the family name to make it more commercially attractive.

O'Cearuill senior has been described as a fiercely ambitious, pushy parent. He is credited with the decision to get JJ out of United in an attempt to fast-track his career.

The family had previously flirted with other major European clubs, including Barcelona. Gabriel even went on a tour of the Spanish club's ground – and was photographed with superstar forward Lamine Yamal.

Former United head coach Michael Carrick said of Gabriel: 'He's a young boy, he's 15 and the biggest (thing) for me definitely and as a club point of view is looking after our younger players – their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure.

'And I think all of us we've got to be really conscious of that, really, in this situation.

'As a club, for sure, we're all involved in those conversations. I just think we've got to be very careful of that.'

#1271. Why U.S. Soccer's move to name Emma Hayes to the USMNT hiring committee makes sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

By the time U.S. Soccer confirmed Mauricio Pochettino's departure for Manchester United early Friday morning, the announcement itself was far from a surprise. The press release included the usual formalities – Steve Cherundolo, the U-23 U.S. men's national team head coach, would fill in for the Dec. 13 friendly against Jamaica that falls outside the FIFA international match calendar, and the assurance that the search for Pochettino's USMNT successor would begin shortly. Federation CEO J.T. Batson and COO Dan Helfrich will unsurprisingly lead the search, as will "the soccer leadership team at U.S. Soccer that includes" assistant sporting director Oguchi Onyewu. There was one unique detail tucked into the announcement, though.

Emma Hayes, the U.S. women's national team head coach, will also have a say in the matter.

Men's and women's national teams rarely overlap at any given federation, largely because there's little need for a crossover event. They operate on different calendars and in the best case scenarios, each team has dedicated members of staff. Hayes' name-drop as news of Pochettino's exit became official, then, is a unicorn-like sighting, even if U.S. Soccer often champions a spirit of collaboration between all of its national teams. It is uncommon for the head coach of one senior national team to help recruit a counterpart but in U.S. Soccer's case, it makes complete sense.

Hayes' coaching career, which spans two decades and two continents, means her inclusion on the federation's soccer leadership team comes as a no-brainer. She is amongst the most respected soccer minds in the game, which easily makes her one of the most important people on U.S. Soccer's payroll no matter how you look at it. That will be especially true in a hiring process that has to conclude with a compelling follow-up act to Pochettino's splashy arrival two years ago. Her perspective might actually be vital in the process, which only adds to the intrigue of what's next for the USMNT.

USMNT coaches are rarely style hires; look no further than the list of people to hold the job on a full-time basis this century and the picture paints itself. The only thing Bruce Arena, Bob Bradley, Jurgen Klinsmann, Gregg Berhalter and Pochettino seem to have in common, outside of the job they all once held, is that they were all tasked with some sort of cultural reset depending on the task at hand. That likely will not be the case for Pochettino's successor, though, who will inherit a team with a clear style of play, a healthy mix of veteran players and rising talents and plenty of time on the clock until the next World Cup. The job will be defined in part by continuity, even with the necessary allowance for the new hire to put their unique spin on things.

That's where Hayes' expertise should play a crucial role, and the same goes for Onyewu. Hayes' tactical know-how makes her as qualified as anyone employed by U.S. Soccer to establish the right stylistic profile for the next USMNT coach, especially with the spirit of continuity in mind. Pochettino's track record with the U.S. team was mixed but at its best, his high-intensity, attack-minded approach suited the player pool really well and continues to do so. Hayes, a tactical pragmatist who prioritized attack-minded teams herself with Chelsea and the USWNT, will be more than able to help match candidates to the player pool they will spend the next several years working with. Hayes admitted as much on Wednesday when addressing the topic for the first time.

"I work really closely with J.T. in particular and even more so with Dan as we're growing to develop the American soccer movement and J.T. asked if I would be involved as a technical voice, to be involved with the process and I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men's national team coach," she said. "My role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job at least, albeit with the women's team, and that I've coached for a number of years and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why and like I said, I feel confident in the group that are being put together. I think it'll be a very thorough process. I think that's the most important part of it and like I said, I feel very embedded in what we're doing with the federation so it doesn't feel unusual to me so, like I've said many times, let's build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that's the important part and let's let's get it right."

That's especially true considering the fact that there are very few slam-dunk candidates to replace Pochettino. Pep Guardiola, months into a sabbatical after a decade with Manchester City, is an obvious target for U.S. Soccer but it is entirely unclear how interested he would be in the vacancy. If he's out of the running, the list of contenders with genuine international appeal dwindles quickly but it does not necessarily mean the list of worthy candidates vanishes with Guardiola. The hiring committee will need to be strategic in that case, both in terms of creating a list of contenders and then narrowing them down over the interview process, Hayes providing an important perspective along the way.

The jobs of the USMNT and the USWNT head coaches are hardly apples-to-apples but even then, one will still have an acute idea of what the other's job entails. There is inherent value in having a coach help in the process of hiring another coach, since they hold such singular positions – they are often treated as the be-all, end-all when it comes to their team's success, fairly or otherwise. She can also speak to the cadence of national teams, which varies greatly from the club game where coaches essentially work with their players every day during a long season.

"Everyone is aware of the major differences between coaching at the club level and international level, and the main difference is just time on the field and time with your players," Hayes told CBS Sports earlier this year when asked about Pochettino. "Every international coach would love to have more time with their team, but that's not the nature of the international calendar and it's something I know we both had to get used to and are still getting used to … I said a few times that it's almost like we are grandparents. We get to see the players for a week or so and then we send them back to their parents, which is their clubs."

Outside of her tactical expertise, though, Hayes represents U.S. Soccer's ambitious turn in recent years as much as Pochettino does. She was hired because of her reputation as a serial winner at Chelsea, where she won eight league titles and seven cups. She continued the trend in short order with the USWNT – two months after officially starting in the role, she won Olympic gold at the Paris Games in 2024. U.S. Soccer has equally ambitious goals for the men's team, though the timeline will understandably be longer for that program. They continue to target the USMNT's first World Cup quarterfinal appearance since 2002 but in between, they also hope to medal in the Olympics' men's soccer event, which is contested by U-23 teams, for the first time when the Games come to Los Angeles in 2028. More than many at the federation, Hayes has experience with the intangibles it takes to reach those heights and that's exactly why she was hired in the first place.

Beyond that, though, Hayes in particular has an idea of what the USMNT job might entail. She is the best of both worlds – she began her coaching career in the U.S. two decades ago and has a deep understanding of the American soccer landscape, but made a name for herself in her native England and can also bring a useful outsider's perspective. There is no perfect equivalent to Hayes waiting for the USMNT job since no coach with experience in the American game has truly broken into the top tiers of the sport just yet, the federation likely to settle for one or the other. Hayes' understanding of both orbits, though, makes her an important guiding force along the way. She might be the only qualified person to answer how much to weigh the insider's perspective with the accomplished outsider's point of view when looking for the next USMNT head coach, in large part because she is the only person who boasts an equal share of it.

Hayes' expertise alone means she will be as valuable a sounding board as any, to the point that it's hard to minimize her ability to offer input down to one or two straightforward things. There is one more thing Hayes might have that no one at U.S. Soccer does – easy access to some of the most notable coaches in the game.

Over the course of her successful 12-year tenure at Chelsea, Hayes became one of the most respected coaches in England. She became the first woman to win the Football Writers Association's Tribute Award in 2024 shortly before leaving England for the U.S., and has earned the praise of many of her counterparts in the men's game along the way. Out of anyone at U.S. Soccer, Hayes might actually have the most compelling list of phone numbers in her contacts. She has said Sir Alex Ferguson, a coaching legend if there ever was one after his storied 27-year tenure at Manchester United, calls her "from time to time." Hayes has been in touch with a handful of her contemporaries over the years, including those who have been on U.S. Soccer's radar at one point or another. In her 2024 book, "A Completely Different Game," Hayes said she heard from Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp after having an emergency hysterectomy because of endometriosis in 2022. The pair "sent me long messages, expressing deeply felt emotions," as did Graham Potter and David Moyes.

The rolodex is a covetable one, if ex-U.S. Soccer sporting director Matt Crocker can serve as an example. His greatest accomplishments during his three-year spell, which came to an end in April when he took a similar role with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation, were hiring Hayes and Pochettino. He had previously worked with Pochettino at Southampton a decade earlier, which made U.S. Soccer's approach easier when discussions started. Hayes' value exceeds her ability to hand her bosses a phone number but it is unlikely to go unnoticed at U.S. Soccer, who clearly understands the expertise she would bring to the search in a variety of ways.

#1269. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. "I want to see relentless consistency from our players, individually and as a team, and I want us to be elite in both penalty boxes. Hayes selected a full roster that features several players competing in their first-ever senior-level World Cup qualifying tournament, and a handful of veterans. Midfielders (6): Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current; 7/1), Sam Coffey (Manchester City, ENG; 46/5), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit FC; 180/40), Claire Hutton (Bay FC; 22/1), Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC; 124/29), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes, FRA; 22/1)

A positional shift to left winger and an outrageous amount of scoring have all led her back to the USWNT due to consistent performances, a key factor for Hayes with her large player pool.

"Be consistent first of all in performance. Ashley Sanchez wasn't on our radar, not because she isn't talented, but there were certain things we demanded from the performance that I think she has delivered in her game on a regular basis. So, I think that's the first thing. I think you've seen that includes Croix Bethune coming into this camp -- been outstanding in the number 10 position all year, and would have been in last camp as well if she was fit. You do have to consistently find consistent performances, particularly if you're a player that doesn't have credit in the bank," Hayes said.

As the World Cup gets nearer, finalizing a roster for the 2027 summer tournament is even closer. Things like consistent form and senior-level experience will come into play when naming a final 23 for the World Cup for Hayes.

"If you're a Mallory Swanson and delivered on a world stage on a regular basis for the national team, it does alter things slightly. No, we don't want players that are in our group that are in a place where they're not fighting to improve every day or be as competitive as they could possibly be, but I think when players have stacked and accumulated a lot of experience over a period of time, that is always going to put them in a steady position," Hayes explained.

"But it doesn't guarantee anything. I will be unafraid to leave anybody off that plane if I don't feel that they are applying themselves to put ourselves in the best possible position to compete. Which is why this upcoming camp, our job is to qualify for the World Cup, and so everything we have worked towards is ensuring that every player that comes in at camp makes sure they lift their level and they position the team to have the most positive outcome, regardless of the opponent. And I'd be demanding as much as I always do, but I have a big expectation from our senior players to step up."

El Salvador is the eighth-ranked team in the Concacaf W Championship and earned its spot following a preliminary qualifying round. The group is coached by manager Eric Acuña, who recently made headlines for harshly criticizing his players in a press conference following losses to Paraguay last month.

Still, Hayes and the staff aren't taking any opponent lightly no matter the rankings or state of the locker room.

"It's a team that knows is competing for something, so it doesn't matter the opponent; they're competing to go to a World Cup, and do I think that will be it will be demanding and taxing? And yes, I do. In many different ways, because the expectations are all on us. I think for them, it's how are they going to disrupt us and make it difficult? But they have two players in the front line that can cause a lot of problems, particularly in transition. So we have to set up for that," Hayes said.

"I think when it when it comes to the players, I've always championed creating positive environments for players. And yeah, I'm sad for the players to hear what they've gone through, but as always, I can't control that. I want the best for players all of the time in their environments, but I am here to represent the U.S. and try and help us qualify for the World Cup. So my focus is on that. Even if my heart goes out to the players and I think we still have a lot of work to do in the women's game to keep driving female-centered, female-lens environments where women can thrive."

Florian Wirtz looks in the mood after a couple of excellent performances for Germany under ex-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp

#1262. Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear

The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time in January 2025, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon rainforest— a key carbon sink — turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.

Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement in late October. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the ability of the nascent carbon removal industry to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.

The UN has warned that any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.

"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, executive director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.

"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

#1259. Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p-wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1,2,3). Achieving p-wave superconductivity4 and its magnetic analogue5—characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p-wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge6,7. Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p-wave magnets5,7,8,9,10, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p-wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves Sy polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted Sy exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics10, topological matter7, superconductivity11 and beyond.

Unconventional symmetry breaking in itinerant fermion systems has revealed some of the most remarkable phases of quantum matter. A celebrated example is p-wave superfluidity in helium-3, where odd-parity Cooper pairing generates emergent orders beyond conventional paradigms1,2,3. Its magnetic analogue, the p-wave magnet, is characterized by an odd-parity spin-polarized electronic structure that preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation while breaking inversion symmetry5,6.

Recently, spin group theory has provided a framework for identifying such magnetic states5, extending concepts developed for altermagnets12. Whereas ferromagnets exhibit conventional s-wave-like spin splitting and altermagnets exhibit even-parity d-, g- or i-wave spin order12,13, p-wave magnets are characterized by odd-parity spin polarization associated with commensurate coplanar magnetic order that breaks inversion symmetry while preserving a combined time-reversal and translation symmetry5,14. The resulting electronic structure can exhibit a single symmetry-allowed spin component, symmetry-enforced nodal planes and a characteristic momentum-dependent spin texture. Candidate p-wave magnetism has recently been explored in insulating NiI2 (ref. 8) and metallic Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12 (ref. 9). However, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the characteristic odd-parity electronic spin texture remains limited8,9.

Here we present evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level (near-EF) electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi by combining symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, neutron scattering and photoemission spectroscopy. Neutron diffraction reveals a commensurate spiral phase with propagation vector (0, 1/3, 0) below the upper magnetic transition temperature, TN1 ≈ 62 K, followed by a transition to a conical phase at the lower magnetic transition temperature, TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Magnetotransport measurements indicate strong coupling between magnetism and itinerant electrons. Below TN1, spin-integrated angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, associated with strong 4f–5d exchange coupling. Spin-ARPES provides spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the expected odd-parity Sy polarization in the near-EF spectral features: the extracted polarization changes sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Because the near-EF spin-resolved features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, the observed Sy modulation is best interpreted as a spectroscopic signature of the expected p-wave spin texture at the level of the reconstructed electronic structure. Magnetic force microscopy (MFM) and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-µm chiral magnetic domains. Together, these observations identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and related spin-symmetry-based phenomena.

In conventional ferromagnets and altermagnets (Fig. 1a), broken time-reversal symmetry permits even-parity spin-polarized electronic structures12. In the non-relativistic limit, conventional ferromagnets exhibit s-wave-like spin splitting, whereas altermagnets can exhibit d-, g- or i-wave-like spin-splitting patterns12,13,15,16,17,18. By contrast, unconventional odd-parity magnets can host p-, f- or h-wave spin polarization that preserves time-reversal (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\))-related symmetry while breaking inversion (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)) symmetry5. Commensurate chiral magnetic structures provide a natural route to such \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)-symmetry breaking. In particular, coplanar non-collinear exchange fields can generate odd-parity spin polarization in momentum space when the magnetic structure preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) (ref. 5). As in conventional antiferromagnets, this symmetry enforces zero net magnetization in the ideal p-wave magnetic state (Fig. 1a).

a, Schematic magnetic orders and their associated s-wave (ferromagnetic), d-wave (altermagnetic) and p-wave spin splitting in momentum space. Magenta and cyan spheres represent magnetic atoms with opposite spin orientations, related by the indicated combined spin–space symmetry operations in the d- and p-wave states, whereas blue spheres represent nonmagnetic atoms. b, Spiral magnetic structure of EuSi. The characteristic p-wave spin group symmetries are spin rotation combined with a glide mirror plane \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}{\bf{t}}]\), and with a lattice translation \([{C}_{2}{||}{\bf{t}}]\), respectively. c, Calculated spin-polarized Fermi surface of the spiral phase, including SOC, showing p-wave spin polarization and spin splitting. d, Calculated spin textures near the top of the valence bands in the kz = 0 (bottom) and kx = 0 (top) planes, with (left) and without (right) SOC. e, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersion along the −Ym–Г–Ym (ky) direction in the spiral phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC. f, Conical magnetic structure of EuSi, with the combined spin-rotation and translation symmetry \([{C}_{6}{||}{{\bf{t}}}^{{\prime} }]\) indicated. g, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersions along the same momentum direction in the conical phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC.

We next consider the symmetry of the experimentally determined magnetic structures of EuSi. The crystal belongs to the point group D2h (space group Cmcm), and its magnetic states without (with) considering the effect of spin–orbit coupling (SOC) are described by the corresponding spin (magnetic) space group7. For the spiral state below TN1 ≈ 62 K, the spin space group is \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{y}}1\), which satisfies the criteria for collinear p-wave spin polarization in momentum space. The spin space group breaks the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\) symmetry, thereby allowing odd-parity spin polarization. The coplanarity of the magnetic moments, together with the spin-only symmetry \({C}_{2y}{\mathcal{T}}=[{M}_{y}|1]\,{=}^{{m}_{y}}1\), constrains the spin polarization to the y direction in momentum space. Combined with the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) symmetry, the spin group symmetry prohibits the spin components Sx and Sz, while allowing a \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\)-symmetric Sy component satisfying:

The spin-degenerate nodal plane at ky = 0, where ky is the component of the electron crystal momentum k = (kx, ky, kz) along the reciprocal-space direction corresponding to the crystallographic b axis, is protected by the combined spin rotation, lattice mirror and translation symmetry \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}t]\), as illustrated in Fig. 1b. The corresponding spin-polarized electronic-structure calculations are shown in Fig. 1c–e. Figure 1d illustrates the calculated p-wave spin–momentum locking near the top of the valence band in the (kx, ky, 0) and (0, ky, kz) planes. The calculated bands obey the symmetry relations:

Here, E(kx,ky,kz,Sy) denotes the electronic band energy at crystal momentum k for a state with spin polarization Sy along the b direction. Comparison of calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 1c–e) shows that the characteristic p-wave spin polarization and splitting arise predominantly from the non-relativistic magnetic exchange, with only minor modifications from SOC. These calculations therefore provide the symmetry and electronic-structure framework for the p-wave state expected from the spin and magnetic (\({P}_{C}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}\)) space groups of the experimentally determined spiral magnetic structure.

We next consider the conical state below TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Its spin space group takes the ferromagnetic form \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{6}_{y}}{t}^{{\prime} }\), characterized by a symmetry combining a six-fold spin rotation with translation, [\({C}_{6y}{|}{t}^{{\prime} }\)], as shown in Fig. 1f. Figure 1g shows the calculated electronic structure without and with SOC. The calculated dispersions of the spiral and conical phases are similar over much of momentum space but differ near the Γ point (Fig. 1e,g). In the conical phase, broken \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\) lifts the spin degeneracy at the Γ point that is protected in the spiral phase (see Supplementary Note 1 for further symmetry analysis). Accordingly, an anomalous Hall response is symmetry-allowed in the conical phase but prohibited in the spiral phase. The magnetic space groups of both phases are chiral.

EuSi crystallizes in space group Cmcm (No. 63; Supplementary Tables 1–3). Single crystals were grown by the Bridgman method. Scanning transmission electron microscopy indicates high crystalline quality with few crystalline defects (Supplementary Fig. 2), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis yielded an Eu:Si ratio of 50.2:49.8, consistent with stoichiometric EuSi within instrumental uncertainty (Supplementary Fig. 3). Two magnetic transitions occur at TN1 ≈ 62 K and TN2 ≈ 33.4 K, together with a weak structural distortion near the structural distortion temperature TS ≈ 60 K (Supplementary Fig. 4). Magnetization measurements along the three crystallographic axes show no pronounced hysteresis (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating the absence of net magnetic moments at zero field. Upon cooling, these phase transitions define two boundaries: from the paramagnetic to the spiral magnetic phase, and subsequently to the conical magnetic phase (discussed later). Upon applying a magnetic field along the crystal’s a, b and c axes (Fig. 1f), the conical magnetic/spiral magnetic state exhibits metamagnetic transitions associated with spin-flop processes, and eventually evolves into a spin-polarized state at high fields (Supplementary Fig. 6c,f,i). Angular-dependent susceptibility further shows a pronounced two-fold magnetic anisotropy (Supplementary Fig. 7).

a, Temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility measured along the a, b and c axes under zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC) conditions, respectively. The magnetic transitions at TN1 = 62 K and TN2 = 33.4 K, and structural distortion at TS = 59.7 K, are labelled. b, Magnetization versus magnetic field along the three crystallographic axes at 2 K and 40 K. The inset magnifies the low-field region, showing no distinct hysteresis. c, Resistivity of crystal S1 with current along a. The residual resistivity ratio, RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K), is approximately 262. d,e, Neutron-diffraction patterns in the (H, K, 1) plane at 40 K (d) and 6 K (e). f, Temperature evolution of the (0, 4, 0) and adjacent k1 satellite peaks between 5 K and 70 K. g,h, Refined spiral and conical magnetic structures at 40 K (g) and 6 K (h). The reference Eu moment in the a–c plane is aligned along a. This convention differs from Fig. 1 by a global rotation within the a–c plane, preserving the relative moment configuration and magnetic symmetry. i, Temperature-dependent intensities of representative k1 and k2 peaks, (0, 5/3, 1) and (0, 2, 1). The dashed lines mark the magnetic transitions. CM, conical magnetic; SM, spiral magnetic; PM, paramagnetic. f.u., formula unit; r.u.l., reciprocal lattice units; Q, scattering vector; j, electrical current density.

The longitudinal resistivity is metallic, with a residual resistivity ratio (RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K) ≈ 262), where ρxx is the longitudinal electrical resistivity (Fig. 2c). A sharp resistivity change near TN1 and pronounced transport anisotropy accompany the magnetic transitions (Supplementary Fig. 8). Magnetotransport measurements further reveal a large, non-saturating magnetoresistance at low temperature (reaching 4,600% at 2 K with a 9 T magnetic field along b) (Supplementary Figs. 9–12). With increasing temperature towards the spiral magnetic state, the magnetoresistance becomes negative and remains so up to room temperature, indicating strong magnetic scattering in both the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic states.

To determine the magnetic structures, we performed single-crystal neutron diffraction (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Note 5). At 40 K, satellite peaks appear at (H, K, L) ± (0, 1/3, 0) (Fig. 2d), corresponding to a magnetic propagation vector k1 = (0, 1/3, 0). Magnetic-structure refinement identifies an spiral magnetic order with moments rotating in the a–c (010) plane (Fig. 2g). The spins are approximately ferromagnetically aligned within each double layer and rotate by π/3 between adjacent double layers, corresponding to a threefold magnetic periodicity along b. This commensurate coplanar spiral is consistent with the symmetry requirements for the p-wave magnetic state discussed above.

On cooling to 6 K, the k1 satellite peaks remain, while additional magnetic intensity develops at the structural Bragg positions, corresponding to a second magnetic propagation vector k2 = (0, 0, 0) (Fig. 2e). Refinement shows that this component corresponds to a ferromagnetic moment along b, yielding the conical magnetic structure shown in Fig. 2h. The persistence of the k1 intensity across TN2 supports the coexistence of the spiral and b-axis components within the conical magnetic phase rather than macroscopic phase separation. The refined ordered moments are mac = 4.4(1) μB per Eu at 40 K and mac = 5.4(1) μB per Eu, mb = 4.1(1) μB per Eu at 6 K, where μB is the Bohr magneton, consistent with the Eu2+ valence inferred from X-ray absorption and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements (Supplementary Fig. 14).

The temperature dependence of representative magnetic peaks further resolves the two transitions (Fig. 2f,i). The k1 order develops below TN1, whereas the k2 component appears below TN2. Critical exponent fits yield β = 0.32(2) for k1 and β = 0.33(3) for k2, slightly below the classical three-dimensional Heisenberg value (β = 0.365), possibly reflecting additional spin–lattice coupling.

Before turning to the spin-resolved measurements relevant for p-wave magnetism, we first characterize the overall electronic structure of EuSi across the magnetic transitions (Fig. 3). The calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the spiral magnetic phase (Fig. 3b) contains several electron/hole pockets exhibiting strong anisotropy along the kx, ky and kz directions. Figure 3c shows the measured band structure in the kx–kz plane, corresponding to the cleaved a–c (010) plane in the conical magnetic phase. The constant-energy contours (Fig. 3c) show clear C2 symmetry and are broadly consistent with the calculated Fermi surface; similar dispersions are observed in the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases.

a, Crystal and magnetic Brillouin zones (BZs) of EuSi, with the projected surface BZ of the a–c (010) cleavage plane shaded above. High-symmetry points are labelled. b, Calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the magnetic BZ in the spiral magnetic phase. c, Constant-energy contours at EF (i), EF − 0.1 eV (ii) and EF  − 0.2 eV (iii) in the kx–kz plane measured at 10 K. d,e, ARPES dispersion along the \(\overline{{\rm{Z}}}-\overline{\Gamma }-\overline{{\rm{X}}}\) direction, measured at 57 eV (ky ≈ 2π/b; d) and corresponding calculated bands (ky ≈ 2π/b; e). Here, b is the crystal lattice constant. f,g, ARPES dispersions measured with 7 eV photons (ky ≈ 2π/b; f) and corresponding DFT calculations at ky ≈ 2π/b (g) in the conical magnetic (i), spiral magnetic (ii) and paramagnetic (iii) phases. The α, β and γ bands are labelled. h, Temperature-dependent energy-distribution curves integrated near \(\overline{\Gamma }\) over the shaded region in f(i). Fitting resolves the peaks associated with α, β and γ. i, Temperature-dependent peak energies obtained from the energy-distribution curve fits. j, Corresponding energy separations between α and γ, β and γ, and α and β. Error bars in i represent energy uncertainties estimated from the energy resolution of the 7-eV laser-ARPES set-up at each temperature; those in j represent the corresponding propagated uncertainties in the energy separations.

The measured dispersion along the corresponding high-symmetry direction exhibits dispersive Eu 5d bands crossing EF (Fig. 3d). The measurement geometry, orbital-character analysis and determination of the high-symmetry points for the a–c cleavage plane are described in Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16. The bands near the \(\overline{\Gamma }\) point are labelled α, β and γ, and the band near the zone boundary is denoted φ, following comparison with the density functional theory (DFT) calculations in Fig. 3e. Differences in the number and precise positions of the calculated and measured bands may arise from the simplified treatment of magnetic structure, calculation parameters such as effective on-site Coulomb interaction U and lattice constant, and many-body effects (Supplementary Note 10).

Over a wider energy range, ARPES reveals the Eu 4f- and Si 3p-derived states (Supplementary Fig. 17). The Eu 4f flat bands, labelled FB1–FB3, lie approximately 1–2 eV below EF and are further identified by resonant ARPES measurements (Supplementary Fig. 18). These states are crossed by dispersive Si 3p bands, consistent with orbital-projected calculations. Their location well below EF is consistent with the localized 4f 7 configuration and large local Eu2+ moment.

The magnetic transitions are accompanied by a pronounced reconstruction of the near-EF electronic structure. High-resolution laser-ARPES demonstrates that the α, β and γ bands evolve strongly across the conical magnetic, spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases (Fig. 3f). Their characteristic energies shift by approximately 50 meV between the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases, followed by a more pronounced reconstruction at TN1, where the three bands merge upon entering the paramagnetic phase (Supplementary Fig. 19). Tracking their energy positions from energy-distribution curve fits (Fig. 3h–j) shows that this reconstruction follows the temperature evolution of the in-plane magnetic order k1 determined by neutron diffraction (Fig. 2i). The calculations (Fig. 3g) reproduce the main evolution in the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases, whereas larger deviations occur in the conical magnetic phase, suggesting that the additional b-axis ferromagnetic component has a comparatively smaller influence on the near-EF electronic structure. Similar evolution of the α, β, γ and φ bands is observed at different photon energies and momentum directions (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21), indicating a robust magnetism-driven reconstruction of the Eu 5d electronic structure.

We attribute this reconstruction to the strong 5d–4f exchange coupling between the localized Eu 4f moments and itinerant Eu 5d electrons through intra-atomic exchange19,20. This exchange lifts the spin degeneracy and accounts for the large band splitting with a gap of approximately 100 meV (ref. 21). Once the spiral magnetic/conical magnetic order develops, the enlarged magnetic unit cell also imposes a periodic exchange potential that folds the reconstructed 5d bands. This interpretation is consistent with the observed substantial Eu moment22. The Si p bands also show reconstruction across TN1, whereas the Eu 4f bands remain nearly unchanged in energy, although the intensity of FB1 starts to decrease at TN2 (Supplementary Fig. 22).

The dominant effect of the a–c-plane magnetic moments is further reflected in the reconstructed electronic structure across multiple momentum planes, arising from the combined effects of exchange splitting and magnetic-zone folding. Consistent reconstruction is observed by ARPES on both the cleaved b–c (100) and a–b (001) surfaces (Supplementary Note 8).

We probe the predicted p-wave symmetry using spin-resolved ARPES on the a–c cleavage plane at 40 K. The relevant symmetry relations predict opposite Sy polarization under \({k}_{y}\to -{k}_{y}\), \(E(0,{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\,=\) \(E(0,-{k}_{y},{k}_{z},-{S}_{y})\) and unchanged Sy under the corresponding \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\), \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) operation. By varying the photon energy, we sample a series of ky values across successive magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4a,b; additional measurements from an independent facility are shown in Supplementary Fig. 34). At \(({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z})\,=\) \((0,0.3\times 2{\rm{\pi }}/b,0)\) (cut 1 in Fig. 4d; b is the magnetic-supercell lattice constant), the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions show negative, positive and negative Sy polarization of approximately 5%, respectively. At the corresponding negative-ky position (cut 4 in Fig. 4d; see Supplementary Note 9 for the band assignment), the extracted polarizations show the opposite signs. For intermediate ky values approaching the nodal plane ky ≈ 0, (also −0.5 × 2π/b) the net Sy polarization is strongly suppressed (cuts 2 and 3 in Fig. 4d), consistent with the node-like behaviour expected for an odd-parity spin texture.

a, Measurement geometry on the a–c (010) cleavage plane. Cuts 1–4 (right) sample momenta along kz at different ky, accessed by varying photon energy; cuts 5 and 6 (left) compare symmetry-related momenta under \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\). Yellow and purple indicate positive and negative reduced ky, respectively, relative to each magnetic-zone centre. b, Extracted Sy polarization of spectral feature labelled α across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The sign-changing modulation and suppression near nodal regions are consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture. The solid curve shows calculated unfolded Sy polarization in the lattice Brillouin zone for qualitative comparison. Vertical lines mark cuts 1–4; high-symmetry points are labelled. c, Calculated Sy polarization of representative valence (val_1 and val_2) and conduction (cond_1 and cond_2) bands along ky in the magnetic Brillouin zone, shown without (top) and with (bottom) SOC. d, Spin-resolved ARPES spectra for cuts 1–4 at kx = 0. Each cut shows the spin-integrated spectrum (left), spin-resolved energy-distribution curves (right) and extracted Sy polarization (below). Dashed arrows mark the δ, α and γ spectral regions. The polarization reverses between positive and negative reduced-ky regions and is suppressed near predicted nodes (ky = 0 and −0.5  × 2π/b). b is the magnetic-supercell lattice constant. e, Spectra for cuts 5 (left) and 6 (right) at fixed ky. The extracted Sy polarization is unchanged within statistical uncertainty under \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\). Error bars in b and shaded envelopes in d and e represent one standard deviation propagated from Poisson counting statistics. These observations are consistent with the predicted spin symmetry but do not establish an eigenstate-resolved test because the measured features contain unresolved band contributions with momentum-dependent spectral weights.

To examine the momentum dependence more systematically, we extract the energy-integrated Sy polarization of the feature labelled α within the fitting-defined integration window at photon energies from 13 eV to 23 eV, sampling successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The extracted polarization exhibits a sign-changing modulation and is strongly suppressed near the ky = 0 nodal regions (Supplementary Fig. 33 and Supplementary Note 9). Despite the finite out-of-plane momentum resolution, the observed modulation is consistent with the odd-ky spin texture expected for p-wave magnetism and with the calculated spin-polarization patterns in both the lattice and magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Figs. 35 and 36). The variation in modulation amplitude across successive zones is also consistent with momentum-dependent unfolded spectral weights, which redistribute contributions from folded magnetic-supercell states at different extended-zone momenta (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 36). The persistence of the same sign-reversal pattern in calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 4c) further indicates that the dominant spin texture originates from magnetic symmetry rather than SOC.

In addition, we find that the Sy polarization of the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions remains unchanged within statistical uncertainty for symmetry-related points (kx, ky) and (−kx, ky), consistent with \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) (Fig. 4e).

We note two limitations of the spin-ARPES analysis. First, the measured polarization is small, approximately 5%, compared with the calculated maximum contrast of about 25% (Fig. 4c), and the clearest spin-resolved features occur at finite binding energies within the near-EF electronic structure rather than at EF. The measured spin polarization may be reduced by finite energy and momentum resolution and by partial cancellation between unresolved contributions with opposite spin polarizations. Averaging over oppositely chiral magnetic domains could further reduce the signal if such domains are sampled within the illuminated area. Second, the near-EF features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, and the cuts at positive and negative reduced ky were acquired using different photon energies and sample different extended-zone momenta, so the relative spectral weights contributing to a measured feature may differ. The measurements therefore do not constitute a one-to-one, eigenstate-resolved test of the calculated symmetry relations. In particular, the present data do not uniquely separate the momentum dependence of individual-band spin polarization from changes in the relative spectral weights of unresolved components. Within these limitations, the sign-changing Sy modulation and its suppression near the predicted nodal regions provide spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence consistent with the predicted odd-parity p-wave spin texture of the reconstructed near-EF electronic structure of EuSi.

The large local magnetic moment and its strong coupling with the electronic structure enable the measurement of the magnetic domains with different chiralities using complementary probes23,24. Figure 5a shows the magnetic domains on the a–c plane measured by MFM in the conical magnetic phase, revealing a bubble-in-stripe pattern with a characteristic width of approximately 10 μm, corresponding to opposite spiral configurations. Similar stripe-like magnetic domains are observed by circularly polarized micro-ARPES with a submicrometre beam spot (Fig. 5b).
